Colorado State.title: 73-7 is rock bottom for CSU football, and more questions than answers from Jim Mora
Colorado State.summary:
Just when you thought CSU football couldn't sink any lower, the Rams delivered one of the most humiliating performances in program history, a 73-7 demolition at the hands of a 1-8 Washington State team. Joel and Mike don't hold back as they examine a historically inept defense, an offense that's suddenly gone missing, and a program that appears to be moving backward under Jim Mora.

The guys take a hard look at Mora's increasingly puzzling public comments, including his claim that CSU doesn't know how to win, his repeated criticism of the previous defensive staff, and a series of contradictory statements throughout the season. Plus, a miserable weekend for Rams basketball and some well-deserved recognition for CSU volleyball's historic Pac-12 championship. A passionate, candid conversation from two diehard supporters who love CSU but believe it's long past time to demand better.

Colorado State.title: Mora's breaking point: What's really going on inside CSU football?
Colorado State.summary:
Following an embarrassing 31-14 loss at Utah State, Jim Mora unleashed a fiery postgame tirade unlike anything we've heard from a CSU head coach in years. He called out his players, coaching staff, the program's culture, and even the university itself, declaring that "the hammer is coming down." Joel and Mike dissect Mora's explosive comments, revisit the baffling decision to retain former defensive coordinator Tyson Summers, and explore whether deeper issues behind the scenes could be complicating CSU's rebuild. They also discuss Amy Parsons' surprising departure as university president, the questions surrounding CSU's commitment to athletics, and what all of this could mean for Mora's future in Fort Collins. Plus, a brief look ahead to a daunting matchup with Boise State and the start of CSU basketball season.

Colorado State.title: The Hauss is back! CSU wins a wild one, but can the Rams keep it rolling?
Colorado State.summary:
After four straight losses, CSU football finally gave fans something to celebrate with a thrilling 56-49 win over San Diego State. Joel and Mike break down the wild shootout, highlighted by Hauss Hejny's spectacular return from injury, accounting for 418 yards and five touchdowns. The guys discuss why Hejny is a game-changer, what CSU must do to keep him in Fort Collins beyond this season, and why this explosive offense makes Rams football more entertaining than it's been in years. The defense remains a mess, but timely turnovers and some improvement against the run helped secure the win. Plus, the guys look ahead to a Halloween road trip to Utah State, where another victory could put bowl eligibility back within reach, and briefly discuss CSU basketball's concerning exhibition loss at San Diego.

Colorado State.summary:
What started with so much promise has turned into a nightmare for CSU football. After opening 2-0, the Rams have dropped four straight, surrendering an astonishing 222 points along the way. Joel and Mike discuss the historically bad defense, Jim Mora's accountability for the ongoing struggles, and whether new defensive coordinator Kenny McClendon can realistically turn things around. But there's still reason for hope. Quarterback Hauss Hejny returns to the lineup Saturday against a San Diego State team that may present CSU's best opportunity in weeks to get back in the win column. The guys break down the matchup, the Aztecs' vulnerabilities, and why Joel is surprisingly optimistic about CSU's chances. Plus, with bowl eligibility slipping away, what will it take to salvage the season and restore some confidence in the direction of the program?

Gonzaga.title: Top-15 prospect Jalen Davis commits to Gonzaga over UCLA, North Carolina, UW: 'I'm looking to win'
Gonzaga.summary:
Jalen Davis kept a live YouTube audience in suspense for a handful of moments Tuesday afternoon before the top-15 prospect and coveted combo guard unzipped a black Adidas pullover.

“I’ll be choosing the University of…” Davis started, inherently creating a few more tense moments for Gonzaga fans watching online through a CBS Sports stream.

“…Gonzaga,” Davis finished, revealing a navy Gonzaga basketball T-shirt before picking up a red “Zags” hat from behind the makeshift scorers table he sat at with family members and coaches.

“Go Zags baby, go Zags!” Davis yelled.

The top-ranked prospect in Washington and 13th-rated player in the recruiting class of 2027 according to 247Sports.com announced his commitment to Gonzaga on Tuesday afternoon, choosing Mark Few’s program over UCLA, North Carolina and Washington.

The Zags have had success rate recruiting the state of Washington over the last three decades and they’ve occasionally swung big on a national level, landing a few of the top 10-20 players in the country.

But Davis might be the first player to fit both categories.

The 6-foot-4, 175-pound combo guard becomes the top-rated player in Washington to choose Gonzaga and the fourth highest-rated recruit in school history. Only Chet Holmgren, Jalen Suggs and Hunter Sallis are listed ahead of the Bremerton High standout on 247Sports.com’s all-time database.

“For me choosing Gonzaga, it was a bunch of things, a lot of big factors,” Davis told CBS Sports. “For one it was the play style and fit. I just love how fast-paced they play. It’s more like a EuroLeague type team. Other factors is the culture. I’m pretty big on culture when it comes to programs and I think it’s also the connection, how we built the relationship with all the coaches. It kind of felt like back at home.”

Before trimming his list to four schools, Davis released a top 10 that included his four finalists along with Texas Tech, Iowa, USC, BYU, Ole Miss, TCU and Stanford.

According to 247Sports.com, Davis is the 13th-rated player in America, the third-rated combo guard in the ‘27 class and the top player in Washington. Another recruiting service, Rivals.com, rates him as the 24th-rated player in the class and the eighth-best player at his position.

Davis won Gatorade Player of the Year honors in Washington in 2025-26 after averaging 31.5 points, 9.6 rebounds, 5.8 steals and 5.2 assists for a Bremerton team that went 26-2 last season en route to its second straight state championship. A two-time Olympic League MVP, Davis made an overtime buzzer-beater to help the Knights hold off Columbia River in the semifinals and knocked down a pair of late free throws to help Bremerton clinch a 45-43 win over R.A. Long in the championship.

Multiple recruiting services list Davis as a combo guard, but according to 247Sports.com’s Eric Bossi, Gonzaga’s coaching staff demonstrated how they could use him on and off the ball during an official visit that coincided with a Nov. 7 home opener against New Mexico State.

Gonzaga will be losing at least five rotation players from this year’s team, including point guards Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett and Nathan De Sousa, potentially creating opportunities for Davis to operate as a lead guard for Few’s program in 2027-28.

The timing of Davis’ commitment is significant, too.

Last October, the Zags picked up a commitment from another top-rated class of 2027 guard, Dooney Johnson, but the Milwaukee native didn’t sign with GU during the early period and is keeping his options open while remaining “publicly committed” to Mark Few’s program, On3.com’s Joe Tipton reported Monday.

“Mark Few’s plans, he wants a guard like me that can really compete at a high level and compete for a national championship,” Davis said. “I think for me coming to the program, I can bring a lot of energy on and off the court, especially on the leadership role. Then want to make me and everybody else better on and off the court.”

Davis is coming off a standout summer on the AAU Adidas 3SSB Circuit, averaging 24.3 points, 5.6 rebounds, 4.5 assists and 2.8 steals per game for Slow Grind Elite.

“The message to Gonzaga is I’m looking to win,” Davis said, “so I’m going to stand on that.”

Davis has maintained a 3.7 grade-point-average at Bremerton and is involved in the running start program at Olympic College, according to 247Sports. He told CBS Sports he plans to partner with Gonzaga on a scholarship fund that will help current and future students with financial aid.

“It’s basically an idea, we’re doing a foundation – it’s an opportunity for current and future Zags for a scholarship,” he said. “It’s just a cool thing to do partnering with Gonzaga.”

Gonzaga.title: Previewing Kansas State, potential Players Era matchups | Zags Insiders Podcast
Gonzaga.summary:
No. 22 Gonzaga is part of a strong field at the Players Era 16 in Las Vegas, beginning with Tuesday’s first-round assignment against Kansas State.

Richard Fox, former Gonzaga center and analyst on GU telecasts, and yours truly sized up the Wildcats and possible second-round matchups against No. 15 Alabama or Baylor on the latest Zags Insiders Podcast.

The entire podcast can be found at https://www.spokesman.com/podcasts/zags-basketball-insiders/ or https://youtu.be/9o09yft7ws0.

Here are a few excerpts.

Wildcats a wild card

Fox: Gonzaga is a 13.5 point-favorite, that feels right to me. Nothing really stands out when you look at their numbers, but I will say their 3-point shooting – they’re top 20 in the country, taking 32.6 on average. They make 36% of them, about 12 per game, and their effective field-goal percentage is pretty good, around 57%.

Guard Brandon Rechsteiner, about 10 of his 14 field-goal attempts per game on average come from 3. Jaden Schutt, seven of his eight attempts come from 3.

Anytime a team shoots the 3-point ball as well as that, it gets your attention. If Gonzaga does a good job guarding the 3-point line, they should be all right.

Meehan: They beat Creighton. I watched that game. Kansas State looked very good, kind of pulled away late. They lost at home (Friday), not a good loss to Campbell.

They have a pretty good guard line. The Zags better get used to that. They’re going to be running into good guard lines. Everybody from here on out has players in the backcourt and the Zags are going to get tested in a big way.

Rechsteiner’s dad is Scott Steiner, WWE famous wrestler. If there’s any stat category on the sheet, Rechsteiner is probably leading it.

Bama or Baylor in second round

Meehan: Alabama is long, guard heavy. Aden Holloway is a 6-1 guard but not a point guard necessarily. He’s very offensive minded. Amari Allen played good against the Zags off the bench last year (in GU’s 95-85 win in Las Vegas), now he’s a focal point. He’s got 30 assists, so he’s a (6-6) point wing if you want to call him that. They want to get up in down and play in the 80s and 90s, shoot a lot of 3s and get to the line.

The free-throw line is going to be very important. Allen is 31 of 38 in five games, 30 assists, three turnovers. He’s pretty physical. Is that going to be (Davis) Fogle guarding him, (Isiah) Harwell? That’s going to be a very interesting matchup.

Baylor came up just short against Texas, which knocked Gonzaga out a year ago in the NCAA Tournament. I wouldn’t blink twice if they beat Alabama in the opening round. They look to be on the way up again.

If it’s Baylor, (coach) Scott Drew and his contingent of bigs have a knack for shutting down Gonzaga’s bigs, namely Drew Timme. They got him in the national title game, held him down (to 12 points, 5 of 7 FG, five turnovers). And they got him (nine points) at the Sanford Pentagon in Sioux Falls. I wonder if he has something plotted for Braden Huff?

Fox: Alabama is unapologetically into the analytics. They’re either going to get to the basket or take 3s. They make 25 free throws per game and 3-point shooting, they’re taking 34 a game and making 13. They’ve got legitimate size. They’ve got kind of a counterweight to Gonzaga’s inside, not quite as big but certainly going to be very athletic.

Holloway is very difficult to match up against. He’s very quick, aggressive, just shoots it so well. They’re going to play super fast. The game will come down to the glass. Can Gonzaga keep Alabama to one shot and done?

Baylor hasn’t played a lot of people other than Texas. Their best offense might be throw it toward the basket area and then go get it. They’re No. 8 in the country at 17 offensive rebounds a game. They’re very good defensively, turning people over almost 20 times a game.

I could say this about a lot of the teams I’ve watched: Arizona, Houston, Texas, Baylor, the physicality of these teams is remarkable. As big and talented as LSU was, this is a different level when it comes to physicality, that size, the aggression, that strength.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga stays put at No. 22 in AP poll with big tests looming at Players Era 16
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga stayed put at No. 22 in this week’s Associated Press Top 25, but the Bulldogs can probably anticipate some movement in the rankings after playing three or four games over the next five days at the Players Era 16.

After beating Montana State 74-62 during a one-game week, Gonzaga was one of just five teams not to move up or down in the latest version of the poll.

Houston claimed the No. 1 ranking in the country, moving up seven spots after beating Florida and Kansas to capture the championship at the Players Era 8, which was held one week before the 16-team Players Era event that’s taking place at T-Mobile Arena and Michelob Ultra Arena over the next five days.

Virginia came in at No. 2, followed by No. 3 Florida, No. 4 Illinois, No. 5 Texas Tech, No. 6 UCLA, No. 7 Texas, No. 8 Arizona, No. 9 Tennessee and No. 10 UConn.

Former Gonzaga assistant Tommy Lloyd and the Wildcats managed to climb four spots after picking up a signature home win over then eighth-ranked UConn at the McKale Center.

That means there will be two top-10 teams and seven ranked teams in total competing this week at the Players Era 16. Along with Texas Tech and Tennessee, the 16-team field will feature No. 13 St. John’s, No. 15 Alabama, No. 17 Miami, No. 22 Gonzaga and No. 25 Louisville. Three other teams in the tournament – Iowa State, Baylor and Michigan – are receiving AP votes.

Gonzaga is still the only team from the Pac-12 Conference in the Top 25, but two others collected votes in the week three poll. Now at 5-0, Utah State appeared on one AP ballot at No. 24 while Texas State received a single vote in the wake of a 7-0 start.

The Zags dropped one spot in the USA Today Coaches Poll, falling to No. 23 on Monday.

Gonzaga.title: Report: Five-star recruit Dooney Johnson remains committed to Gonzaga while exploring other college options
Gonzaga.summary:
Dooney Johnson, the only current member of Gonzaga’s 2027 recruiting class, declined to sign with Mark Few’s program during the early period and is exploring other potential college options, according to a report from On3.com’s Joe Tipton.

Johnson, the No. 14 prospect in the country according to Rivals.com, remains committed to the Zags for the time being, but “has been willing to engage in conversations with other schools,” Tipton reported Monday.

It was notable that Johnson, who committed to the Zags on Oct. 29, 2025, declined to sign a binding agreement with the school during college basketball’s early signing period, which runs Nov. 11-18. The 6-foot-5, 185-pound point guard had previously listed himself as a “Gonzaga commit” on his Instagram bio, but recently removed the title from his profile.

Johnson still has a commitment graphic up on his Instagram profile from when he pledged to the Zags last year and Tipton reaffirmed the point guard from Milwaukee is still “publicly committed” to Few’s program.

But Johnson, who recently transferred from Milwaukee Juneau High in his hometown to East River High in Orlando, Florida, continues to weigh his options and has participated in Zoom calls with other schools, according to Tipton.

Johnson’s five-star rating makes him the fourth highest-ranked recruit in school history, behind only Chet Holmgren, Jalen Suggs and Hunter Sallis, according to 247Sports.com.

According to Rivals, Johnson is not only the 14th-rated overall prospect in the country but the fifth-rated point guard and sixth-rated player in the state of Florida.

Before transferring high schools this offseason, Johnson led Milwaukee Juneau to a state championship in Wisconsin while averaging 27.8 points, 8.5 rebounds, 4.7 assists and 3.4 steals.

Playing this summer for Team Herro, the Nike EYBL AAU team sponsored by Milwaukee Bucks guard Tyler Herro, Johnson averaged 14.9 ppg, 4.4 rpg, 3.0 apg and 1.1 spg. He led Team Herro to an 18-4 record during the summer circuit and a trip to the semifinals of the popular Peach Jam tournament held in Augusta, Georgia.

During a conversation with The Spokesman-Review this summer at Nike EYBL in Las Vegas, Johnson spoke about his relationship with Gonzaga’s coaching staff and indicated he was excited to play for the Zags starting in 2027-28.

“Just got to be patient, but I’m always ready to go be at Gonzaga,” he said. “Great program, great coaches. Especially coach Few, he was really great when I went there. B-Mike (assistant Brian Michaelson), that’s my guy. So yeah it’s going to be good.”

Davis to make commitment

There could be more major news for Gonzaga this week on the recruiting front.

Jalen Davis, a Bremerton High School standout and Gonzaga target considered to be one of the top 15 prospects in the country, is announcing his college commitment at 2:30 p.m. Tuesday afternoon during a live show with 247Sports and CBS Sports. The commitment will air on the CBS Sports college basketball YouTube channel.

The 6-foot-4 combo guard is choosing between Gonzaga, Washington, North Carolina and UCLA. Davis recently took an official visit to Gonzaga for the team’s home opener against New Mexico State on Nov. 7.

According to 247Sports, Davis is the 13th-ranked prospect in the class of 2027, the nation’s third-ranked combo guard and the top-rated prospect in the state of Washington.

Gonzaga.title: Brandon Rechsteiner's outside shooting should have Gonzaga on notice against Kansas State | Key matchup
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – One way or another, Gonzaga was going to deal with Brandon Rechsteiner and his potent outside shooting this season.

Rechsteiner went from a conference opponent to a nonconference opponent for Gonzaga when the former Colorado State guard transferred to Kansas State this offseason – one of 10 Division I transfers Casey Alexander signed shortly after the former Belmont coach was hired in March.

The jury’s still out on Kansas State’s roster after the Wildcats lost a season opener to South Dakota State and dropped their second home game to Campbell on Friday, but Rechsteiner has unquestionably been a bright spot since moving to Manhattan, Kansas.

Few players in the country have been better from behind the arc than the 6-foot-1 guard.

Rechsteiner, who played two seasons at Virginia Tech before transferring to Colorado State, is leading Kansas State with 19.2 points per game and tied for fifth in the country at 4.5 3s per game, sitting not far behind former Gonzaga wing Steele Venters, who’s averaging 4.7 3s for Washington.

Rechsteiner’s 3-point percentage has gradually improved throughout his career, too. The Georgia native made 27.3% as a freshman at Virginia Tech before improving to 29.9% as a sophomore and taking a huge leap as a junior at Colorado State, where he connected at a 40.0% clip. It’s only been five games, but he’s on track to set a new career high, making 42.3% of his 3s at Kansas State.

The Zags will have to be conscious of Rechsteiner’s whereabouts at all times on Tuesday. The senior guard set his career high in consecutive games this season, scoring 26 points on 6 of 15 from the 3-point line against Cal State Northridge before scoring another 26 on 6 of 12 from distance against Creighton.

“He’s a lot of fun to watch, but he gets it honestly, he works for it,” Alexander said after the Creighton game. “He really puts in the time. I’ve known him for a long time. I knew he was a confident kid and a tough kid and a winner. Just does things that allow him to win. So I’m not really surprised. He’s playing great, but I’m not really surprised. That’s why we brought him here.

“I told him I wanted him to come to K-State and play 30 minutes a game and start at point guard and be our leading scorer. So glad it’s working out that way so far.”

Rechsteiner is also a productive rebounder for his size, hauling in 4.8 boards per game to go with a team-high 4.0 assists.

Each of Gonzaga’s three point guards – Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett and Nathan De Sousa – should get turns guarding Rechsteiner. The Zags may also call on shooting guard Isiah Harwell, their top on-ball defender, to help with the Rechsteiner matchup if the guard gets going early.

Gonzaga.title: Kansas State, Players Era 16 field to provide stiff test for Gonzaga's perimeter defense
Gonzaga.summary:
LAS VEGAS – In no particular order, Izan Almansa and Braden Huff identified rebounding, turnovers and offensive execution as the non-negotiable items Gonzaga would need to address at practices before traveling to Las Vegas to take on a daunting three- or four-game schedule this week at the Players Era 16.

“I would say if we do that, we’re more than fine,” Almansa said after Gonzaga’s 74-62 victory over Montana State last Tuesday. “The last game we had it, then we started not executing, not boxing out. So be physical and execute on offense too.”

Another item probably emerged as the 22nd-ranked Zags started doing their homework on Kansas State and the cluster of teams they could encounter during their second trip to the loaded Thanksgiving week tournament taking place this week at T-Mobile Arena and Michelob Ultra Arena.

Gonzaga’s first game in Vegas – and the tournament at large – will be a stress test for the Bulldogs’ perimeter defense, another area of concern for Mark Few’s team after conceding 20 3-pointers in the last three halves of basketball against Montana State and LSU.

Kansas State brings the worst KenPom rating (No. 102) into this week’s bracket-style tournament, but even the Wildcats (3-2) are capable of throwing a wrench into Gonzaga’s plans if the Bulldogs (3-1) don’t make the right defensive adjustments before Tuesday’s 9:30 p.m. (ESPN) tipoff at T-Mobile Arena.

It hasn’t been a clean run for first-year coach Casey Alexander, with “buy game” losses to South Dakota State and Campbell already on Kansas State’s resume, but the Wildcats have been one of the nation’s top outside shooting teams, ostensibly giving them the chance to stay in any game.

Kansas State ranks No. 17 in the country at 11.8 made 3s per game and still may not be the top 3-point offense the Zags see this week in Las Vegas. Alabama, a potential second-round opponent for Gonzaga, sits No. 3 nationally at 12.8 3s per game. If the Zags don’t match up with the Crimson Tide on Thursday, they’d face Baylor and transfer guard Brett Decker, who currently leads all Division I players at 4.8 3s per game. Creighton and Michigan, two of the four teams the Zags could see in their third game, are tied at No. 27 in the NCAA both averaging 31.8 3-point attempts per game.

In the season opener, Gonzaga conceded a number of quality looks to Purdue, but the Boilermakers finished just 5 of 21 from the 3-point line, airballing multiple attempts down the stretch. New Mexico State didn’t hurt the Zags from behind the arc, going just 4 of 14, but LSU and Montana State combined to go 24 of 56 (42.8%) in the two games that followed, capitalizing on missed coverages and blown defensive assignments.

“We’ve got to get better this week, we’ve got to take advantage of this time off to get better both offensively and defensively,” Huff said. “It’s fun, you play those games, you play really good teams on short turnarounds and I’m looking forward to it, excited for the challenge. But got a lot of prep, got to take advantage of this, take time to get better and go down there and execute it to win.”

Three-point defense will be a big key on Tuesday, but the Zags expect to be challenged in other ways during a weeklong gauntlet that will see them play three games in four days, or potentially four over a five-day span if they advance to Saturday’s championship.

“It’s a really, really solid, talented group of teams and it’s three games in four days so you have to prepare for like anything and everything,” Few said. “You can play against a team that zones you for 40 minutes and the next game you might play against a team that presses you and just plays up-tempo. Then the last game might be a 50-48 grinder.”

Gonzaga had a full week on the practice court after games against LSU and Montana State. It’s been a much quicker turnaround for a Kansas State team that had plenty to correct after shooting 27 of 77 (35%) from the field during an 80-70 loss to Campbell on Friday.

Alexander’s starting five is exclusively made up of Division I transfers, led by former Colorado State and Virginia Tech guard Brandon Rechsteiner, who averages 19.2 points on 42.3% shooting from the 3-point line. Wing Isaiah Abraham, who previously played at Georgetown and UConn, is the second-leading scorer averaging 13.0 ppg.

Prior to Kansas State, Alexander coached seven seasons at Belmont, six at Libscomb and two at Stetson. Few and Alexander are two of four coaches in the country to win at least 20 games in 10 consecutive seasons – the others being Kansas’ Bill Self and Houston’s Kelvin Sampson.

Gonzaga’s coach urged fans to support the team in Vegas after Purdue had an overwhelming advantage in the bleachers when the teams met down here three weeks ago.

“It’ll be a great tournament, we’ll have great competition and hopefully we’ll get some Zag fans down there,” Few said. “Our last trip to Vegas, there were a lot more Purdue people than there were Zag fans. So hopefully they’ll rally down there.”

Gonzaga.title: Inconsistent Gonzaga women fall to California at North Shore Classic
Gonzaga.summary:
The inconsistency continued for the Gonzaga women’s basketball team Monday afternoon.

Scoring droughts and stretches of turnovers were too much to overcome for the Bulldogs, who fell 71-60 to the unbeaten California Golden Bears in the North Shore Classic in Oahu, Hawaii.

Guard-heavy Cal, which improved to 7-0, is the best team the Zags have played. Gonzaga went scoreless for 5 minutes, 34 seconds late in the third quarter and committed five turnovers during that stretch.

The Bears made 5 of 8 from 3-point range in the third, and a 3 extended their lead to 45-36 and capped a 9-0 surge.

Gonzaga junior forward Lauren Whittaker ended the scoring slump with a basket inside, pulling the Zags within 45-38 with 39 seconds left in the period.

A 3-pointer by Teryn Gardner and another basket from Whittaker cut Cal’s lead to 47-43 with 8:20 remaining. But Gonzaga continued to struggle finding baskets and the Bears pushed their lead to 58-47.

A 3-pointer from Allie Turner and a basket by Whittaker allowed Gonzaga (4-4) to trim Cal’s lead to 58-52. But the Zags wouldn’t get any closer the final 3:25.

Cal forward Naya Ojukwu – who played nine games at Gonzaga in the 2023-24 season before leaving school at the semester break – scored back-to-back baskets as the Bears pushed the lead back to double digits.

Whittaker had her fifth double -double of the season and 18th of her career with 20 points and 13 rebounds. She also had five assists. Turner had 12 points and three assists and Taylor Smith added 10 points.

Gonzaga shot 37% from the field, making 23 of 62. The Zags made 23 of 63 in their win over Hawaii on Saturday.

Gonzaga is off until Sunday when the Zags make a short trip to face Eastern Washington.

Gonzaga.title: Players Era 16 primer: Breaking down all seven teams Gonzaga could face next week in Vegas
Gonzaga.summary:
It’s called the Players Era 16 but feels a little more like the Sweet 16 when you factor in the talent, brand-name programs and coaches taking part in the Thanksgiving week event held over six days at T-Mobile Arena and Michelob Arena in Las Vegas.

The path to a Players Era championship for No. 22 Gonzaga (3-1) starts with Tuesday’s late-night tipoff against Kansas State (3-2) at T-Mobile Arena (9:30 p.m., ESPN).

After an off-day, the Zags will return on Thanksgiving to play either No. 16 Alabama or Baylor, with No. 17 Miami, No. 18 Michigan, TCU and Creighton as potential third-round matchups on Friday. The second- and third-round games will also take place at T-Mobile Arena, the same venue where Gonzaga opened the season with a 78-72 win over Purdue.

If Gonzaga survives that minefield of opponents with a 3-0 record, Mark Few’s team would face one of eight teams from the opposite bracket in Saturday’s 7:30 p.m. championship at Michelob Arena: No. 9 Texas Tech, No. 13 St. John’s, No. 14 Tennessee, No. 23 Louisville, Oregon, Iowa State, Maryland or San Diego State.

For now, we’ll preview the group of teams Gonzaga could play Tuesday, Thursday and Friday, with snapshots of all eight potential opponents in Vegas.

Tuesday – first round

Kansas State (3-2)

Coach: Casey Alexander, first season

The outlook: The Alexander era in Manhattan, Kan., got off to inauspicious start when Kansas State dropped its season opener to South Dakota State, 68-66. The Wildcats then rallied for three straight wins, including a victory over the Creighton team Gonzaga will see in a few weeks’ time, before taking another tough “buy game” loss to Campbell on Friday. Kansas State is looking to beat opponents from the 3-point line, ranking No. 20 nationally in attempts per game while connecting at a 36% clip as a team.

Who to know: As of Saturday, just five players in the country were making more 3’s per game than Kansas State senior Brandon Rechsteiner, who averages 4.4 per game on 10.5 attempts and a 3-point clip of 42.3%. No surprise here, but the Colorado State transfer who started his career at Virginia Tech also leads the Wildcats in scoring average at 19.2 points per game.

Thursday – second round

No. 16 Alabama (5-0)

Coach: Nate Oats, eight seasons

The outlook: If Gonzaga struggles to contain Kansas State 3-point offense, it could be another long night on day two if the Bulldogs match up with the Alabama team they beat in this event last season. Alabama’s personnel will look slightly different, but the Crimson Tide still boast one of the nation’s top offenses, rating No. 4 in KenPom’s adjusted efficiency metric and No. 6 in total 3-pointers per game at 12.8. The Tide may still be vulnerable at the other end of the floor after allowing 91 points in a recent win over Kennesaw State.

Who to know: Guards Aden Holloway (16.3 ppg) and Amari Allen (16.2 ppg) do a lot of the damage for Oats’ team, but eight players average between 8.0 and 16.3 ppg. A 6-foot-6 point guard, Allen is the most versatile player on Alabama’s roster and a potential NBA lottery pick who’s also averaging 6.0 assists and 5.0 rebounds.

OR

Baylor (4-1)

Coach: Scott Drew, 24 seasons

The outlook: Gonzaga and Baylor have played seven times since Few and Drew have been at the helm of their respective schools, but never during Feast Week. Baylor had been to six consecutive NCAA Tournaments before last year’s miss, but the Bears are right back in the mix this season with a new-look team that obliterated four “buy game” opponents and took No. 7 Texas down to the wire last Sunday. Baylor could be at a slight disadvantage against Gonzaga with a smaller lineup, but the Bears have been disruptive on defense, ranking No. 6 nationally with 19.8 forced turnovers per game.

Who to know: Pick your poison with Baylor’s backcourt. Brothers Kayden and Dylan Mingo average a combined 27.8 points, 9.6 rebounds, 7.2 steals and 4.4 steals for the Bears, but 6-foot guard Brett Decker Jr. has been the one pacing Baylor’s offense at 17.4 ppg. The Liberty transfer is averaging 4.8 3-pointers per game after a 35-point eruption against Jackson State that saw him make 10 of 17 shots from deep in just 26 minutes.

Friday – third round

No. 17 Miami (5-1)

Coach: Jai Lucas, second season

The outlook: The Hurricanes haven’t faced much resistance since a season-opening loss to top-ranked Florida, winning each of their last five games by 20 points or more. Miami brings one of the nation’s top defensive teams to Vegas, allowing just 57.0 ppg and limiting opponents to 33.3% from the field. Both of those numbers rank No. 6 nationally.

Who to know: With five leading scorers through their first five games, the Hurricanes become a difficult team to scout. Shelton Henderson received most of the preseason accolades and the former top-30 recruit is leading Miami in scoring (13.2 ppg), rebounding (8.2 rpg) and steals (1.8).

OR

No. 18 Michigan (3-1)

Coach: Mike Boynton, first season

The outlook: Dusty May’s 2025-26 team made a statement with a 101-61 win over Gonzaga in this event last season, but the group returning to Sin City this week will look nothing like the one that won a Players Era title and captured the national championship five months later. The Wolverines don’t have the same size across the front line but don’t confuse them as small. If the rematch happens on Friday, Gonzaga’s frontcourt should be in for another challenge facing, Michigan’s 7-2 JP Estrella and 6-11 J.P. Estrella.

Who to know: Trey McKenney was a key sixth man for Michigan last season, scoring 17 points off the bench against Gonzaga. The sophomore guard has expectedly stepped into a larger role this season and is posting solid numbers across the board, averaging 17.0 points to go with 4.3 rebounds and 3.0 assists. Backcourt mate Elliott Cadeau hasn’t found his rhythm offensively, but he had 13 assists in the Gonzaga matchup last season.

OR

TCU (4-1)

Coach: Jamie Dixon, 11 seasons

Outlook: The recent addition of fifth-year Saint Louis transfer Robbie Avila makes TCU one of the more interesting teams in the Players Era field, but the Horned Frogs won’t be considered one of the favorites in Vegas. TCU struggled in multiple buy games against Louisiana-Monroe and Milwaukee before picking up its first loss of the season against Texas A&M in overtime. TCU’s offense has posted at least 92 points in four of games, but the defense is still getting up to speed after allowing 92 points against ULM and 97 against Texas A&M.

Who to know: Avila won Atlantic 10 Player of the Year honors last season at Saint Louis and could become TCU’s most impactful player by the start of Big 12 play, but junior guard Micah Robinson has been the Frogs’ go-to scorer up to this point, averaging 18.0 ppg with 4.2 rpg, 2.2 apg and 2.0 spg. Robinson’s reached double digits in all five games, scoring a career-high 27 points against ULM. He’s also been somewhat turnover-prone, registering at least three in four of the five games.

OR

Creighton (4-1)

Coach: Alan Huss, first season

Outlook: Gonzaga could get an early look at the Creighton team they’ll visit in Omaha on Dec. 12. The Blue Jays, now under the direction of former assistant Alan Huss, rebounded from their only loss to Kansas State by narrowly beating Iowa, 70-69, five days later. Creighton returns one starter, forward Jackson McAndrew, from the team that lost 90-63 at the Kennel last season, and the Jays have been generally balanced while rating No. 39 in adjusted defense and 64 in adjusted offense.

Who to know: Guard BJ Davis isn’t leading the Jays in scoring – that’s been Wes Enis, at 15.4 ppg – but the San Diego State transfer has probably been Creighton’s best overall player through five games, averaging 14.0 ppg, 4.2 rpg, 2.8 apg and 2.4 spg. Davis, who started and had 15 points in SDSU’s loss to Gonzaga at Viejas Arena two years ago, spearheaded Creighton’s offense against Kansas State, scoring a season-high 25 points on 6 of 14 from the 3-point line.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga team short-changed on summer reps 'still getting up to speed' after first four games
Gonzaga.summary:
Make no mistake, Braden Huff believes in the long-term potential of Gonzaga’s 2026-27 roster. He’s also cognizant of the gulf that exists between what the Zags have shown through four games and the level of consistency they’ll need to find by March to qualify for their 29th straight NCAA Tournament and make a deep run when they get there.

Someone nitpicking Gonzaga’s first four games – a narrow win over Purdue, a comfortable victory against New Mexico State, a gut-wrenching loss to LSU and a shaky win over Montana State – could point to erratic 3-point shooting or inconsistent 3-point defense. When the Zags resolved their rebounding problems on Tuesday against Montana State, they uncovered a new issue after committing 16 turnovers. Combinations, rotations and even the starting lineup continue to be a work in progress.

But the biggest shortcoming Gonzaga faces less than three full weeks into the season won’t be found on the box score, nor can the Bulldogs fast-track their way to a solution with a few practices or film sessions.

“A bunch of these guys, we didn’t know if they were going to be eligible or not. It’s a new group, we’re still figuring it out, we’re still getting up to speed,” Huff said. “I think we’ve got all the pieces we need and we’ll be good. We’ve just got to figure it out, learn each other’s tendencies and I think get right.”

Cohesion is usually one of the top issues college basketball teams face in mid-November, and all but a few of the 365 that compete in Division I had a longer runway to establish it than a Gonzaga roster that didn’t come together until after the academic semester started on Aug. 31.

If the Zags have looked disjointed or disconnected, consider that just three of the team’s nine rotation players were on the court when summer workouts started in early June – a juncture of the offseason when point guard Mario Saint-Supery was still a big part of GU’s plans and 5-in-5 transfers Xaivian Lee (Florida), Chauncey Wiggins (Florida State) and Javon Bennett (Dayton) hadn’t materialized as possibilities to fill out the back end of Mark Few’s 15-man roster.

Huff, Gonzaga’s top returning scorer and only returning starter, still wasn’t cleared for full-contact practice in June, not that the Bulldogs would’ve had the numbers necessary to conduct full, 5-on-5 intrasquad scrimmages anyway.

Returning sophomore Davis Fogle and Big 12 transfers Isiah Harwell (Houston) and Massamba Diop (Arizona State) were the only current rotation members participating in practices during the early summer period. Those three were joined by reserve forward Parker Jefferson, freshmen Luca Foster and Sam Funches and walk-ons Carter Nilson and Alonzo Metz. To help with their numbers problem, the Zags occasionally called on former players Adam Miller and Noah Haaland for 5-on-5 runs.

Even when Huff was cleared in August, he still needed a window to establish an on-court connection with Fogle, who was buried on Gonzaga’s bench when the productive forward went down in January with a season-ending knee injury. Late-arriving international signees Izan Almansa and Nathan De Sousa showed up in mid-July and late-August, respectively, followed by the trio of fifth-year transfers that didn’t report until early September.

All of the circumstances now contribute to a Gonzaga roster that ranks No. 53 nationally in D-I experience but just 237 in minutes continuity at 13.7%, according to a KenPom metric that determines what percentage of a team’s minutes are played by the same player from last season to this season.

Montana State had a discernible advantage in that department Tuesday, and it showed in a back-and-forth game the Zags were able to close out down the stretch. With 10 returners and 65.7% of their scoring back, the Bobcats rank No. 13 at KenPom with 54.8% minutes continuity. Montana State couldn’t match up from a size, physicality or skill standpoint, but the Bobcats ran crisp offensive sets that constantly created open looks from the 3-point line and kept the Zags on their toes for 40 minutes.

“We’ve got some time to kind of reinforce everything and we’re still playing catch up, not having the summer and everything,” Few said. “We’re still playing a little catch up, but obviously need to clean some stuff up on offense.”

After one of the most chaotic offseasons in program history, it was unrealistic to expect the Zags would be a fully baked product by Thanksgiving. Ideally, Few’s team will learn from the growing pains administered by quality nonconference opponents, coalesce during the Pac-12 schedule and hit its stride in March in time for conference and NCAA Tournaments.

The Zags have seen that go the other way. In 2024-25, a Gonzaga team ranked No. 10 at KenPom in experience and No. 4 in minutes continuity came out of the gates swinging, dominating Baylor 101-63 in the season opener. The Zags proceeded to lose four nonconference games, drop four more in WCC play and enter the NCAA Tournament with a No. 8 seed, bowing out with a second-round loss to Houston, raising questions as to whether they may have peaked too early.

Two years removed from that experience, Huff is hopeful this team can follow a different development arc. For now, he’ll continue to exercise patience as the Zags focus on the short-term fixes they can make before next week’s trip to Vegas.

“We’ve got a week until our next game,” Huff said, “so I think we’ll have a chance to clean some of that stuff up and figure it out.”

Gonzaga.title: Rebounding improves, other areas regress for Gonzaga in Montana State win | Rewind
Gonzaga.summary:
Mark Few was only halfway satisfied with Gonzaga’s defensive execution on Tuesday night against Montana State in a game where nothing looked entirely clean for 40 minutes, but everything worked well enough to send the Bulldogs home with a 74-62 victory.

“Pleased temporarily, or at times,” was how Gonzaga’s coach put it after the Bulldogs gave up 12 3-pointers to Montana State but held the Bobcats to 10 of 26 shooting from inside the arc and limited them to just six more points from the free throw line.

Few’s satisfaction level with the defense – “pleased temporarily” – could probably apply to a number of other categories from Tuesday’s game and the young season at large. We take a look at some of the good and bad in today’s Gonzaga-Montana State rewind.

Way to rebound

With positional size across the board, a towering frontcourt and the flexibility to roll out a jumbo five-man lineup with three players standing 6-10 or taller, rebounding seemed to be an area where the Zags could excel in 2026-27.

Up until Tuesday, it had been hit and miss on that front.

The Zags narrowly won the rebounding battle against Purdue (34-31), barely edged a smaller New Mexico State team (30-26) and matched LSU on the glass (42-42) in Saturday’s loss at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Rebounding was one of the few columns Gonzaga won convincingly on Tuesday, more than doubling up undersized Montana State for a 47-21 advantage, including a 15-5 edge on the offensive glass.

“I think especially after Saturday, a big emphasis for us was just being physical, winning those 50/50 balls, just imposing our will,” Gonzaga’s Braden Huff said. “Some of that physicality was a big thing and I think the rebounding was much better tonight.”

Huff has been Gonzaga’s leader on that front this season, averaging a career-high 6.8 rebounds per game at the moment. Aside from a rare zero-rebound effort against New Mexico State, the senior forward has pulled down at least seven rebounds in all four games, snatching a career-high 13 against LSU.

“Rebounding has everything to do just with effort and energy and toughness and making something happen,” Few said. “… But that’s just a competitive senior making plays. I think we talked about – we were really disappointed with how we rebounded down the stretch against LSU, it cost us the game. So the guys responded and it was definitely our best rebounding effort of the year.”

Point guard carousel

Gonzaga’s coach urged reporters and fans not to read into the starting lineup switch the team made against Montana State, replacing Xaivian Lee – the starting point guard against Purdue, New Mexico State and LSU – with fellow fifth-year transfer Javon Bennett, who had flashes of excellence on both ends of the floor in Saturday’s loss.

“Don’t get caught up in starting lineups,” Few said. “We’re just going to play – we’ve got a lot of equal guys, so yeah, don’t get caught up in starting lineups.”

Bennett started and Lee came off the bench, but it’s possible a third player, senior Nathan De Sousa, had the best game by a Gonzaga point guard against Montana State.

De Sousa scored nine points on 4 of 5 shooting with one steal and three turnovers in 16 minutes off the bench. Lee wasn’t as efficient, scoring eight points on 2 of 5 shooting, and contributed to Gonzaga’s turnovers with four of his own, but made up for it with six assists and seven rebounds in 24 minutes. Bennett struggled throughout, going scoreless on 0 of 4 shooting with one turnover in 11 minutes.

Few was encouraged by De Sousa’s toughness and physicality in a game where the Zags needed both attributes to emerge with a victory.

“He gives us that toughness and kind of that grit and kind of an older guy and he’s great in there in games like this,” Few said. “This was kind of a fistfight. Really, really physical and they were letting everybody play. Lot of grabbing and holding and that’s when Nate’s at his best. He really helped us tonight.”

Gonzaga continues to experiment and tinker with lineups and rotations early in the nonconference season. At times on Tuesday, Few played Lee and De Sousa together, giving them two ball-handlers who can lead the break and set up GU’s offense.

“Each of those guards bring something different,” Few said, “so you’re going to shuffle the deck through and see who’s playing well this particular game.”

Searching for an identity

On the first two offensive possessions against Montana State, Gonzaga went high-low as Massamba Diop caught the ball near the free throw line before feeding to Braden Huff under the basket.

The Zags converted on the first attempt, failed on the second and didn’t really go back to the high-low, big-to-big look for the remainder of the game.

Gonzaga’s guards, wings and centers will continue to look for Huff in the low-post – the bread and butter of Few’s offense – but the Bulldogs have had trouble establishing an identity otherwise, perhaps no surprise for a team integrating seven new players into the rotation.

“We’ve been working on that and we’ve been trying to have that as our identity, but sometimes teams overplay that and they know we’re trying to do that and this game we forced it a little bit so we need to have some counters and execute what the coaches told us to execute,” backup forward Izan Almansa said. “Because if we do that, we’re going to be fine.”

As Huff started to settle into a groove the last three games, sophomore wing Davis Fogle began to experience some efficiency issues. Fogle combined for 44 points the first two games, but he’s totaled just 31 the last two, making 11 of 27 shots from the field while going 2 of 9 from the 3-point line.

Gonzaga’s teamwide 3-point shooting struggles came into focus against LSU and Montana State (9 of 39, 23%) after the Bulldogs posted outstanding numbers against Purdue and New Mexico State (19 of 40, 47%).

Gonzaga.title: Turnovers slow down Gonzaga's offense in win over Bobcats
Gonzaga.summary:
Massamba Diop grabbed an offensive rebound but lost his balance in the paint and flung an errant pass that was fielded by Gonzaga’s coaching staff on the sideline.

Diop immediately raised his arms upward in frustration. After trotting to the defensive end, he slapped the McCarthey Athletic Center court with both hands.

He was not alone in the frustration department. Roughly two minutes later, Xaivian Lee capped a disjointed second-half possession with a swift, interior pass that was too hot to handle for Izan Almansa. The ensuing play had a similar result: Lee again drove the right edge of the lane but his pass out top was easily intercepted by Montana State’s collapsing defense.

Gonzaga’s offense endured a couple of program rarities Tuesday – extended scoring droughts and turnover-plagued possessions – during a 74-62 victory over Big Sky Conference preseason favorite Montana State.

It’s essentially become a GU trademark to play with pace, inside-outside in the half-court and rank among the nation’s top scoring offenses while posting low turnover rates.

Turnovers hadn’t been a problem for the Zags with just 23 in their first three games. The Zags held a decisive edge in points off turnovers in that span, 66-25, but the Bobcats had the upper hand, 18-10, in that category by capitalizing on Gonzaga’s 16 turnovers.

“Taking care of the ball is something since I’ve been here that we take pride in at Gonzaga,” said senior forward Braden Huff, who joined Chauncey Wiggins as the only Zags with a zero in the turnover column. “Being able to get shots on our terms is a big thing, a big part of our offense.

“When you’re turning the ball over and not even able to get a shot up, it’s an issue. That’s something that we’ll address and figure it out. We’ll clean it up for sure.”

Huff and Almansa both mentioned that ball security will be high on Gonzaga’s to-do list as it prepares for three games in four days, beginning with Kansas State on Tuesday at the Players Era Festival in Las Vegas.

Growing pains are almost a given with seven newcomers in Gonzaga’s current nine-man rotation. “We’re still figuring it out,” Huff said.

The shorter Bobcats packed the paint to try to slow down Huff. The senior forward still hit 7 of 9 shots and 6 of 6 free throws while scoring 21 points, but GU was guilty of forcing several passes inside with multiple defenders surrounding Huff.

“They were switching a lot of stuff and jamming a lot of stuff, and we weren’t getting to the second, third and fourth actions,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said of the turnovers. “When we did that, we kind of had our way with them.

“But when we tried to make something happen on that first side, it works once and kind of reinforces a bad behavior and guys keep trying to do it. That to me, was the biggest key.”

Lee led the Zags in assists (six), but also in turnovers (four). Lee had a couple of longer stretches on the court with fellow point guard Nathan De Sousa, who contributed nine points but had three turnovers.

The Zags finished with a season-low 13 assists.

Gonzaga.title: Lisa Fortier ties record for wins as Gonzaga head coach after team beats Montana 84-61
Gonzaga.summary:
It took a little more than 13 seasons and Lisa Fortier is now tied as the winningest women’s basketball coach in Gonzaga history.

Her Bulldogs gave her victory No. 316 Wednesday, tying the coach (Kelly Graves) she succeeded in 2014-15.

Coming off back-to-back road losses, Gonzaga started better and finished well, handling the Montana Grizzlies 84-61 before 4,752 people at McCarthey Athletic Center.

Fortier’s record is 316-87. The Zags were 316-136 in 14 years under Graves.

It was appropriate that Fortier got No. 316 in the Kennel, where she’s in her 20th season overall. She assisted Graves for seven years before he left for Oregon. Fortier’s record at McCarthey Athletic Center is 158-23.

“It’s just a testament to the players and coaches we have here at Gonzaga and the support we get from the fans,” Fortier said. “I was able to be here for a lot of Kelly’s (wins). The program is storied and we’ve been an important part of the community for a long time – that’s partially because of all the success we’ve had and all the players who’ve come through here. … I’m grateful for that.”

Gonzaga improved to 3-3. It’s been an up-and-down start for the Zags, who returned five starters and five other lettermen.

“I would just say that we’re growing,” Fortier said. “We still have a lot of growing to do. I think the players think we should have picked up right where we left off. We haven’t had (Jaiden Haile, foot injury) and there has been some change on the team. The moral of the story is that it doesn’t matter why (slow start). Like we’re just trying to grow.”

Standout junior forward Lauren Whittaker had her best game of the young season with another double-double – 25 points and 14 rebounds. She made 10 of 11 shots from the field. She also had three assists and two steals and drew nine fouls.

When Gonzaga has been difficult to slow down it’s because it has had offensive balance. Whittaker had lots of support Wednesday. Graduate guard Ines Bettencourt had her best all-around game, scoring a season-high 16 points to go with four steals and the usually team-inspiring defense. Junior guard Allie Turner added 13 points and four assists and freshman forward Abby Lusk came off the bench with 10 points, eight rebounds and two assists in 15 minutes. And junior guard Teryn Gardner, who hit three 3-pointers, added nine points and two steals.

Gonzaga had 15 steals to go with 20 assists. But the Zags committed a season-high 23 turnovers, seven over their average coming into the game.

The Zags led comfortably start to finish. They went into halftime up 40-26. A 5-0 surge to start the third quarter got things going in the second half.

Lusk scored a fastbreak layup to give Gonzaga its biggest lead at 67-39 early in the fourth.

“We’ve had a lot of growth in six games,” Whittaker said, echoing her coach. “Despite our last loss (67-65 at Stanford), we saw a lot of growth and development and how we played together and as a connected team. (Tonight) we played well, played connected, hustled on defense and had some great Zag plays. If we just continue to keep stacking them we will be really effective going forward.”

Before the game, Fortier presented Turner with a ball commemorating her for scoring her 1,000th career point

Montana sophomore guard Paige Lofing, who transferred from Gonzaga in the spring, came in averaging 16.8 points. But the Zags paid special attention to her, limiting Lofing to six points.

Lake City High graduate Avery Waddington hit back-to-back 3-pointers in the second half for the Grizzlies (1-4), finishing with 13 points.

Gonzaga heads to Hawaii this weekend for the North Shore Classic. The Zags take on Hawaii on Saturday and conclude with California on Monday.

Gonzaga.title: WBB Documentary Series Without Limits: Episode Two
No. 22 Gonzaga holds off upset-minded Montana State 74-62 | Analysis
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga’s traditional postgame celebrations still took place near half court. A swarm of players crowded Braden Huff when the senior forward was named the game’s most valuable player, fresh off 21 points and seven rebounds. The Zags traded high-fives with each other and acknowledged fans still lingering around at McCarthey Athletic Center.

But as soon as they disappeared into a tunnel, the celebrating turned right to troubleshooting.

Three days after a wobbly finish against LSU, Gonzaga had to withstand a few more stretches of unsettling basketball against Montana State.

The 22nd-ranked Bulldogs shrugged off a nine-point deficit early in the first half, navigated a prolonged offensive drought in the second and survived a late scoring spree from the Bobcats to emerge with a 74-62 victory in their final game before next week’s trip to the Players Era 16 in Las Vegas.

The product wasn’t pretty, but the result was just what Gonzaga needed 72 hours after letting a 13-point lead slip against LSU and losing a high-profile nonconference game in heart-wrenching fashion at Numerica Veterans Arena.

Tuesday’s opponent may not have been a SEC contender with size and skill at almost every position, but Gonzaga players and coaches knew Montana State would be sneaky tough, bringing its experienced roster and unique offensive philosophies to the Kennel.

“I knew it was going to be a real tough kind of scrappy, hard-nosed kind of battle especially the way Montana State plays,” Gonzaga coach Mark Few said. “They just run that five-out where I knew our guys would be out running around, chasing 3-point shooters. Actually for long stretches of that game I thought we did a nice job defending them. Just the second half our offense was kind of really, really choppy and let them get back into it.

“They did a great job getting back into it, but then we held them off and win. They’re going to have a heck of a year and they get all those guys back from last year, so they’re clicking and in late-season form.”

Montana State shot its way into an early 13-4 lead on a 3-pointer from Cavin Holden, a Longview, Wash., native and former Central Washington standout who finished with a Division I career-high 23 points.

The 3-point line also helped the Bobcats claw back into the game late in the second half, likely evoking a few unpleasant memories of Saturday’s game against LSU for Gonzaga fans.

After going nearly six minutes without a field goal, Gonzaga clung to a five-point lead with 7 minutes, 15 seconds remaining before Davis Fogle, Izan Almansa and Nathan De Sousa delivered layups on four consecutive possessions to open a double-digit lead.

It didn’t close the door on Montana State – at least not completely – and the Bobcats got two more 3-pointers from Howie Keene and Darnez Slater, along with a free throw from Jaden Steppe, trimming the deficit to eight points with under two minutes to play.

Huff, who led Gonzaga in scoring for the second straight game, followed with a jumper at the other end to stretch the lead back out to 10 and Fogle sealed the victory with two more free throws.

Fogle finished with 16 points on 6 of 14 shooting and Almansa was Gonzaga’s third double-digit scorer, recording 12 points and six rebounds. Gonzaga made a switch in the starting lineup, replacing Xaivian Lee with Javon Bennett, but it was another point guard, De Sousa, who led the position group in scoring, totaling nine points on 4 of 5 shooting.

“They’re a really good team, they run really good stuff and they shoot it really well,” Huff said. “I wouldn’t be surprised if they’re in the (NCAA) Tournament, but definitely some stuff we’ve got to clean up. They hit a lot of 3’s on us, so got to be able to take that away and just offensively I think at times it got stagnant and bogged down. So just got to figure that out.”

Gonzaga didn’t shoot the efficiently, making 26 of 54 (48.1%) from the field and 4 of 20 (20.0%) from the 3-point line, but turnovers may have been a larger issue in a game where the Bulldogs committed 16.

Gonzaga also gave up 12 3’s to a Montana State team that finished 40% from the 3-point line.

Gonzaga.title: Late lapses in LSU loss and Chauncey Wiggins' role | Zags Basketball Insiders Podcast
Gonzaga.summary:
Gonzaga appeared to be on its way to a 3-0 start to the season, but some late gaffes turned an eight-point lead with less than three minutes remaining into an 81-80 loss to LSU at the buzzer.

Richard Fox, former GU center and analyst on Gonzaga telecasts, and yours truly sorted through Saturday’s agonizing final minutes, Chauncey Wiggins’ role in the rotation and numerous other topics in the latest Zags Insiders Podcast.

Find the entire podcast at spokesman.com/podcasts/zags-basketball-insiders/ or youtu.be/pQ2aNhKkrMc.

Here are a few excerpts from Monday’s podcast.

Late-game issues

Fox: The Zags were up nine, 77-68, with 3:49 left. They had the game. The offensive rebounding was just killer. These two things are correlated. Offensive rebounds in the first half, Gonzaga with 11, LSU with just three so second-chance points was GU 10, LSU 2. But then you flip it in the second half, 14-7 advantage for the Tigers in second-chance points and a lot of those came down the stretch.

I said this earlier in the year: The college game is a guard-driven game. When you have a guy like (Donovan) Dent, who is not a perfect player, but he is an exceptional college point guard. He doesn’t get sped up, he knows where the ball needs to go, he’s able to score enough where you have to defend him, which makes his pick-and-roll game really difficult to defend.

That was the thing down the stretch, it felt like LSU had a guy to go to that would keep everything calm and control the game, the ball found the right guys at the right spots. And then you couple that with the offensive rebounding, where if they miss or you’re doing a good job against the initial attack, now you’re giving up another opportunity and sometimes two in the same possession.

At that level of basketball, that’s a backbreaker.

Meehan: Gonzaga did 90% of the hard work and just didn’t finish the job. It felt a little like Purdue: led most of the way (against) a very structured, tough-to-play Purdue team, led by 11 in the second half and it got close, closer than it should have. The Zags did enough to win it.

The difference is LSU is a lot more capable than Purdue, they’ve got those guards and that big kid (Michael) Ruzic is terrific. Bottom line, the Zags had to meet LSU more than halfway for this upset to happen.

Twice the Zags gave up rebounds after missed (LSU) free throws and paid both times. Another sequence: Ruzic got a pair of offensive rebounds, hits (Abdi) Bashir for a 3. Several times, the Zags kind of lost assignments defensively. (Davis) Fogle got lost on one, gave up a 3, (Izan) Almansa got lost on one, (Xaivian) Lee over-helped on one and gave up a 3.

Then the bizarre stuff. Lee stumbles on an inbound pass, falls down, travel. (Nathan) De Sousa is in as a defensive replacement, he’s trying to hound Dent (on LSU’s last play), he fell down. Alertly, Wiggins shifted over to guard Dent, you have to guard Dent. Dent creates a little space, just enough to get a 3-point shot over Wiggins, bang.

Wiggins’ fit with the ZagsMeehan: Chauncey Wiggins is eligible, he got through the court process on Thursday. He’s 6-11, long, wiry, good 3-point numbers everywhere he’s been. He was at Florida State (last season).

He hit one 3 (vs. LSU) and was immediately part of the rotation. He played 12 minutes, probably got a couple shifts in each half. A different entity than what they have with the 3-ball ability and that length. I think you can add him to the ‘4’ man rotation but I do think there will be times he can actually play the ‘3’.

He has been practicing. He did look pretty comfortable with things. It felt like he was up to speed. I think there’s a role there, and I talked to somebody on the staff a week or two ago, he’s the kind of guy with that skill set who could get in a tournament game and hit two or three 3s in a half and really flip things for you. He could put up 15 on three or four 3s.

Fox: Ton of experience, three years at Clemson, last year at Florida State, so played at a really high level in the ACC. He’s played in 130 games, 129 coming into this year, started over half of them. You really like that experience. He’s very long, 6-11, 225.

Last year averaged 13 points a game. What he is, he’s a stereotypical stretch big and I think he’s athletic enough to probably play the 3 when they want to go big. He’s not a high-level rebounder. You look at what he’s done career averages, under one assist per game, 27 career blocks and 29 steals. He’s not a super dynamic defender, really a disruptor.

He’s a very solid player on both ends and more importantly, his 3-point shooting profile is super appealing. His career average is 37.5%, never shot worse than 35%, about half of his shots come from behind the arc over the course of his career. You can play him with two bigs, we saw that in both halves, and it’s going to work.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga shuffles starting lineup, bench contributes to win over MSU | 3 takeaways
Gonzaga.summary:
Three takeaways at the buzzer from No. 22 Gonzaga’s 74-62 win over Montana State on Tuesday at the McCarthey Athletic Center.

Bennett gets starting nod

Gonzaga made a change in its starting lineup for the first time of the young season. Fifth-year senior Javon Bennett replaced fifth-year point guard Xaivian Lee in the first unit.

But it was Lee and third point guard Nathan De Sousa off the bench that spurred Gonzaga’s rally from an early 16-6 deficit.

Lee had six points and four assists and De Sousa had his best stretch of the season with seven points and a steal as GU surged in front 41-28 at the break. Lee’s plus/minus in the first half was plus-23 with Izan Almansa right behind at plus-22.

Bennett went scoreless in 11 minutes. Lee finished with eight points, seven rebounds, six assists and four turnovers. De Sousa added nine points.

Bennett has started 126 times in 140 career games, including one season at Merrimack and three years at Dayton. He averaged a career-best 15.8 points last season and earned first-team All-Atlantic 10 honors.

Bench brings it in first half

Three days after being outscored by LSU’s bench 34-17, Gonzaga’s backups delivered 23 points in the first half alone and was largely responsible for the Zags’ 13-point halftime advantage.

Their production slowed considerably in the second half, but the final tally was still heavily in favor of Gonzaga: 32-18.

Almansa paced the reserves with 12 points and six rebounds, followed by De Sousa’s nine points.

Zags cash in at the line

Gonzaga’s offense sputtered mightily at times in the second half, hitting just 1 of its first 11 field-goal attempts.

The Zags were able to get production elsewhere, mainly the foul line. Montana State committed its seventh foul with 14:36 remaining, leading to frequent trips to the free throw line for the Zags.

GU was 12 of 14 before Davis Fogle misfired on a pair with 3:50 remaining. Fogle bounced back by hitting a pair at the 1:02 mark as the Zags finished 14 of 18, offsetting their 9-of-26 shooting from the field.

Gonzaga was 18 of 25 overall at the line. Braden Huff was 6 of 6 and Lee made all four of his attempts. MSU was 6 of 10.

Gonzaga.title: Taylor Smith upping her aggressiveness in second season with Gonzaga: 'I'm growing in a lot of ways'
Gonzaga.summary:
It’s a shot that Taylor Smith would have deferred a year ago.

It came in an entertaining back-and-forth game at Stanford on Sunday.

The Gonzaga senior forward made a 4-foot shot, banked behind her head, giving the Zags a 36-31 lead just before halftime.

As it turned out, it was Smith’s worst shooting percentage through five games. But here’s the deal : She’s shooting more this season.

Smith takes high-percentage shots. She doesn’t take bad shots.

The truth is she could take more shots. But she plays within herself and the offense.

Smith knew her second year at Gonzaga would be better than her first. She barely left her handprints on the first season.

Still, the 6-foot-2 Smith started every game in her first season after transferring from Weber State. She ended up averaging 5.6 points, 3.7 rebounds and 2.7 assists.

This came after a sophomore season when she led Weber State in scoring and was named to the All-Big Sky Conference First Team – the first time the school had a player named to the all-conference team since 2017-18.

Smith, who grew up in nearby Pocatello, Idaho, decided it was time to move on. She wanted more development as a player, entered the transfer portal and contacted a handful of schools.

She had an in at Gonzaga where Bulldogs assistant Jordan Green was familiar with her game. She contacted Gonzaga and arranged a visit.

“I came on my visit and I loved it,” Smith said. “I decided to commit on the visit.”

She is grateful for her time at Weber State.

“I got to play right away – which I was very grateful for my freshman year,” she said.

Smith wanted to be challenged, though. She has found that at Gonzaga.

Admittedly, though, she was tentative last year.

“It was definitely a lot different than what I was used to. It was just more intense,” Smith said. “The pace was definitely something different. I had a lot to learn. I was just kind of figuring out my role and seeing where I fit in and seeing what I could do for my teammates and my team. Being aggressive kind of came later.”

The good news is it has come. Through Gonzaga’s first three games, her attempted shots doubled from a year ago. She averaged 11.3 points, 4.7 rebounds and 2.7 assists in the opening stretch.

“We all knew that she had the potential to be like that,” junior forward Lauren Whittaker said. “She’s got a year under her belt. You see that confidence blooming now, seeing the reps I see in practice in the game has been really beneficial not only for our post players but our team in general.”

With many teams playing more four-guard lineups, Smith often has to step out and defend smaller, quicker players.

Last year she made game-altering blocked shots in two games. She finished with 20 blocks after tallying 61 in two years at Weber.

She also made 24 3-point attempts her first two seasons, but made just 1 of 17 last year and has yet to shoot one this season.

Her game, though, flourishes in the midrange. When Smith is at the top of the key in high-low sets, she’s first looking to pass to Whittaker inside. She knows she needs to look to shoot as an option, too.

Her teammates welcome her to shoot.

“She’s got a deadly midrange game,” Whittaker said. “And she can finish under the hoop. I’m just excited to see how she goes for the rest of the season.”

GU coach Lisa Fortier is thrilled with the uptick in statistical contributions from Smith.

“She’s been really aggressive, which is what we’ve pushed her to be,” Fortier said. “We’ve been lucky enough to recruit really good midrange jump shooters and she’s amongst that group. She’s got a really nice touch around the basket as well.”

Fortier has challenged Smith to be a more active rebounder.

“The area that she’s continuing to grow is as a rebounder,” Fortier said. “I don’t think it’s her favorite thing to do. But she knows that it matters. The best thing I like about her now is she can guard. It’s really nice to have a player like Taylor who can defend the perimeter.”

The new 5-in-5 eligibility rule means Smith has a graduate season she can use. She plans to do so.

Smith says fans will continue to see a better version of herself as the season progresses.

“Now that I know more of my role, I’m just trying to be more aggressive,” she said. “I have the offense down better – where we want to get the shots and where we want to run our offense. I’ve just been trying to hone in on the details. Knowing my teammates’ strengths and weaknesses and they know mine, it’s really nice. It takes a lot of weight off. It’s one less thing I have to think about running up and down the court.”

She’s becoming the player her coaches envisioned. And she’s getting outside of her box.

“I’m very comfortable inside my box, but the coaches are always telling me to get out of my box,” Smith said. “So I’m growing in a lot of ways in a lot of different areas. The coaches are really helping me with that.”
