Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women rally behind defense to beat North Dakota State 62-56
Gonzaga.summary:
It hasn’t been often the last couple of years that defense was the most critical element to victory for the Gonzaga women’s basketball team.

The Bulldogs needed all the defense they could muster Monday until they found some offense late.

Gonzaga didn’t get its first lead until midway in the fourth quarter, but it was all Zags until the final buzzer in a 62-56 win over the North Dakota State Bison before 4,464 at McCarthey Athletic Center.

The Zags forced most of NDSU’s 17 turnovers. They pestered Bison shooters often.

Maybe Gonzaga coach Lisa Fortier was prophetic when she had her team do an interesting drill two weeks ago. She said they put bubbles over the baskets to simulate not being able to make shots.

“We put a rebounding bubble on both hoops so that we could see how we responded when the ball wasn’t going in the basket,” Fortier said. “It couldn’t have been more apropos for the way that the game was going. We are such a good offensive team and the ball was not going in the basket.”

The Zags found themselves in a shooting funk for the first 20 minutes. But good starts to both quarters in the second half went far in Gonzaga finding its way offensively the final 20 minutes.

Gonzaga trailed by as many as 11 points in the first half, but found a way to stay within single digits by halftime.

Three times the Zags pulled within a point in the third, but a late surge allowed NDSU to take a 41-34 lead into the final period.

“We were able to guard well enough and not freak out and try to go one on one and do it all by ourselves,” Fortier said. “We were able to contest shots and to rebound. And that carried us until the tie where we obviously knocked down quite a few baskets.”

The No. 1 shooting team in the nation in 3-point percentage last year, Gonzaga struggled mightily from distance. The Zags had made just 2 of 14 before junior guard Teryn Gardner, who stepped into the starting lineup for the first time in her career, gave the crowd something to get loud about.

Gardner hit back-to-back 3-pointers, pulling the Zags into a 45-all tie and then giving Gonzaga its first lead with 5 minutes, 15 seconds remaining in the fourth.

Junior guard Allie Turner took a nice pass over the top of the defense from junior forward Lauren Whittaker and made a 3, pushing Gonzaga to a 57-51 lead with 1:13 to go.

“Defense was a key aspect for us and being able to get over those screens,” said Whittaker, who finished with a double-double – 22 points and 10 rebounds to go with four steals and two assists. “Communication is what really kind of got us through towards the end.”

Gardner, who made 3 of 8 from 3-point range, finished with nine points and four assists.

“People get so many shots up a day (at practice) that you have to keep shooting,” Gardner said. “It’d be a letdown if you stopped shooting.”

Whittaker said there was a simple explanation for the poor first half offensively.

“We were a little bit disjointed,” Whittaker said.

The Zags never found their touch in the opening 20 minutes. The Bulldogs missed their first seven attempts from 3-point range until Gardner converted with 44 seconds to go before halftime, pulling the Zags within 29-22.

The Zags made 10 of 28 from the floor (35.7%) in the first half, but finished 25 of 61 (41%). They made 5 of 18 (27.8%) from behind the arc.

A 3-pointer from Asp Karrington gave the Bison their biggest lead, 21-10, at the 6:49 mark of the second.

Gonzaga senior forward Taylor Smith hit a couple of big shots in the second half, finishing with 10 points and four assists.

NDSU lost two starters to injuries in the first half including fifth-year forward Avery Koenen, who was named the Summit League’s Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year last season. They were on crutches in the second half.

Gonzaga plays the second of three straight at home Friday when Idaho, an NCAA Tournament qualifier last year, visits.

Idaho opened Monday with a 71-47 win over NCAA Division II Saint Martin’s.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women expect challenge from experienced North Dakota State team
Gonzaga.summary:
When the Gonzaga women’s basketball players step on the court Monday at McCarthey Athletic Center, forgive them if they feel like they’re looking at a team similar to themselves.

In many ways, the Zags will be.

Gonzaga takes on North Dakota State on the first day college men’s and women’s teams may play games. Tipoff is at 6 p.m.

The teams met in Gonzaga’s 2025-26 season opener in Fargo, North Dakota – a game the Zags won 81-66.

NDSU went on to win the Summit League championship and finish 29-5 overall. The Bison return five starters and eight letterwinners.

Sound familiar? Gonzaga returns all five starters and five other key returners off a team that was 24-10, won the West Coast Conference title and conference tournament and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

“They’re really, really good,” GU coach Lisa Fortier said. “They’re just as veteran as we are.”

In the opener a year ago, Gonzaga led 60-38 through three quarters before the Bison pulled closer in the final period. Four Zags finished in double-figure scoring, led by Allie Turner with 18 points on 4-of-5 shooting from 3-point range. Zeryhia Aokuso had 14 points, Lauren Whittaker, in her first collegiate game, had 13 and nine rebounds in 18 minutes and Ines Bettencourt added 12 points and four assists.

The Zags will have to keep many eyes on NDSU 6-foot-3 senior forward Avery Koenen, who had 17 to lead the Bison against GU.

Like Whittaker, Koenen is on the Becky Hammon Mid-Major Player of the Year preseason watch list. She was the Summit League Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year. She’s been tabbed as the league’s preseason POY.

“(Koenen) is one of the best in the country,” Fortier said. “She was one of five players in the country who were the Defensive Player of the Year and the Player of the Year. They have really good guards around her.”

Koenen led NDSU in scoring last year, averaging 19.4 points and 10.8 rebounds. She was the only player in the country last year to average at least 19 points, 10 rebounds and shoot 63% or better.

“They’re kind of like us outside of Spokane, right?” Fortier said. “Everybody in Spokane knows how good they are, but other people don’t. We’re going to have to defend their guards who are tough and gritty. They’re feisty. They can shoot it from the perimeter. They’re athletic. Koenen is an issue that you have to address at all times when she’s on the court.”

Fortier says Koenen wins most one-on-one battles with forwards.

“So we’re going to have to dig in,” Fortier said.

The game is the first of three straight home games for the Zags. GU welcomes Idaho, an NCAA Tournament qualifier a year ago, on Friday and UC Riverside visits on Sunday.

Gonzaga.title: How Gonzaga women have bucked the revolving door trend in new era: 'We recruit uniquely'
Gonzaga.summary:
In a time when a premium is placed on player retention and roster rebuilding, we give you the antithesis: Gonzaga women’s basketball.

At the same time college basketball seems to shift with each change in wind direction, Gonzaga coach Lisa Fortier longs for the old days. Back when building a roster began and ended with high school freshmen.

COVID-19 and the recent 5-for-5 eligibility change has thrown wrenches into the formula in which Gonzaga was built on.

Gonzaga desires that its foundation includes high school players. When the program started making a name for itself in the mid -2000s, the Zags were signing high school players. Before Fortier and continuing during her watch, Gonzaga has followed that formula. Recruit and sign high school athletes, take time to develop them and ultimately reap the benefits.

“We recruit uniquely,” Fortier said. “We’ve never been the group that just amasses talent. We’ve tried to find the right pieces to fit in together. And there is some movement … you can only control so much of that. But we take good care of them. We surround them with people you want to hang out with.”

Fortier has seen it up close for two decades. She’s beginning her 13th season as the Zags’ head coach and 20th overall.

It’s not a coincidence that many programs across the nation have had to eschew the once -traditional means of developing and sustaining their teams – through the signing and development of high school players – for quick fixes brought on by graduation or losses in the transfer portal – in hopes of remaining competitive and not falling behind the winning curve.

Gonzaga has stayed ahead of the curve.

Go back two decades when Gonzaga came on the mid-major scene and started giving teams from power conferences all they could handle. The Bulldogs had an occasional transfer back then, but the bedrock of their success has always been homegrown talent.

Along came COVID-19 followed by name, image and likeness – all of which threw recruiting cycles out of whack. Now comes the initiation of the 5-in-5 eligibility model.

“We used to write out on a whiteboard four or five seasons (rosters) and what that looks like,” assistant coach Craig Fortier said.

Gonzaga doesn’t do that anymore.

“What Lisa promotes is ‘Let’s bring in great people that can get better,’ ” Craig said. “And if we can keep them, then they will get better. We’re always going to be excited to have them as long as we can have them. We never want to have somebody that we’re kind of happy when they head out the door.”

Four of five starters on Gonzaga’s Super Seniors team in 2023-24 were prized high school recruits, developed over four or five years. Interestingly, though, it created some roster consternation. The last two recruiting classes have brought in four freshmen, one of whom transferred out this spring. The 2026-27 roster features one freshman. And the Zags have one commitment for the 2027 class.

How many more players Gonzaga will need to bring in next year depends on how many seniors exercise a fifth-year option created with the new eligibility format.

Seniors Taylor Smith, Zeryhia Aokuso and McKynnlie Dalan – each of whom transferred to Gonzaga – may opt to play another year, transfer for their final season or walk away from basketball.

This year’s roster features six juniors who could play three more seasons including this season. Junior Lauren Whittaker, who was listed on the roster as a redshirt freshman a year ago, is now listed as a junior to be in compliance with the new eligibility rule.

Seven of Gonzaga’s 13 players are transfers. No previous roster has had more transfers.

Thankfully most of Gonzaga’s transfers over the years have had at least two years of eligibility and in some cases three and maybe four.

Of the current group of transfers, Dalan could end up playing four at Gonzaga after spending her freshman season at the University of Minnesota. Former Mead three-sport standout Teryn Gardner could spend four years with the Zags.

Fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt, who hopes a temporary injunction granting her another year eligibility holds up this season, transferred from UConn to Gonzaga two years ago.

This year’s transfers – junior guards Emmy Roach (Rider) and Jocelyn Medina (Denver) – could spend three seasons at Gonzaga.

“So they’ve started to become our guys in our culture because we’ve had them for a while,” Craig Fortier said. “No matter if they’re a transfer or a freshman, the pattern is always going to be development. The more time you get with them, the better generally you’re gonna do. But we’re also trying to be effective and efficient with whatever amount of time we have with them in getting people up to speed with how we want to play and how we think we can help them be the best versions of themselves. That’s always evolving.”

Technically, the Zags have two scholarships available by NCAA rule. But Gonzaga has never had 15 on scholarship at one time.

Gonzaga has a commitment from Gonzaga Prep point guard Aylah Cornwall, who will sign during the early signing period in November. She will essentially fill Bettencourt’s scholarship.

Lisa Fortier says she and her staff continue to recruit for the class of 2027. That’s largely because it’s not known who will exercise a fifth-year option or perhaps transfer. Fortier always wants to have a scholarship in her back pocket.

“We aren’t done with (the 2027 class) yet,” Fortier said. “Most coaches right now are not just taking any high school kid. They have to be a really good fit or a really talented player.”

Gonzaga coaches have been out and about recruiting this fall. The Zags just offered AnnaClaire Bugbee, a 6-2 forward from Mandan, North Dakota, a position in the class of 2028. Bugbee posted a photo of herself with Gonzaga’s coaches on social media recently.

Fortier and her staff are recruiting players for 2028 and 2029.

“We’re recruiting all the time – it never stops,” Fortier said. “Our best players were high school recruits. They are homegrown. That’s a recruiting model we’re comfortable with. It’s hard to place a value on those program kids. You can point to programs like ours where you grow them up, take good care of them and you coach them well. And when they stay they’ll give everything. That’s the kind of people you want on your team – as many of them as you can.”

Gonzaga.title: Loaded Gonzaga women will be team to beat in rebuilt Pac-12
Gonzaga.summary:
The Gonzaga women’s basketball team should discover that many hands make lighter work this season.

Like 10 sets of hands – and maybe a couple more sets depending on the impact of transfers and a freshman.

All five starters return from a team that finished 24-10 and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

Truth is the Bulldogs have seven players capable of starting. And the other three will likely give coach Lisa Fortier pause when it comes to doling out playing time.

The Zags’ abundance of talent begins with 6-foot-3 forward Lauren Whittaker, who broke onto the scene last year as a redshirt freshman and was a force that West Coast Conference teams couldn’t contain. She was named the WCC Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year.

Whittaker is listed as a junior on this year’s roster. Gonzaga is being compliant with the NCAA’s new eligibility rules. Whittaker, who has exhausted a redshirt and used a medical waiver, can play three more years.

She led the Zags with 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game less than a year after having knee surgery. There’s no telling what Whittaker can do with a second year of strength added to her knee.

“It’s been so nice not to rehab anything,” Whittaker said. “I’ve gotten to work a lot on my fitness and stamina. I didn’t really get a summer workout session (last year) because I was just rehabbing the whole time.”

Floating on the perimeter and causing opponents frustration is junior guard Allie Turner, who will start for a third straight season.

An All-WCC first-team selection, Turner was the second-leading 3-point shooter in the nation last season and key to Gonzaga finishing as the top 3-point shooting team, a spot ahead of powerhouse UConn. Turner shot 47.1%, making 89 of 189. The Zags converted 39.2% (244 of 623).

Turner averaged 14.8 points, second best, and 3.5 assists per game.

It was thought Gonzaga would need to replace just one starter. But guard Ines Bettencourt, who graduated last spring, has been granted a fifth season through the NCAA’s new 5-in-5 eligibility model. Bettencourt and 70 other player plaintiffs in the California-based Glancey vs. NCAA lawsuit were granted a preliminary injunction by a California Superior Court judge. She’s still potentially awaiting final clearance from the courts.

A transfer from UConn, Bettencourt, one of Gonzaga’s best defensive players, averaged 6.3 points, 3.4 rebounds and 3.1 assists per game.

Bettencourt became a strong voice among teammates last season. That should continue this season. She’ll get some assistance from Whittaker and Turner.

The Zags’ other two returning starters, seniors Taylor Smith (forward) and Zeryia Aokuso (guard), had flashes of brilliance last season. Smith should be much more effective and dangerous teaming with Whittaker in the high-low sets, and watch for Aokuso to play the point at times and create offense with her ability to get to the rim.

Forward Jaiden Haile, who was named the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year as a freshman last year, and junior guard Teryn Gardner played key roles off the bench. They would start for many teams, and don’t be surprised if either steps into a starting role at some point this year.

Senior forward McKynnlie Dalan, junior guard Christabel Osarobo and sophomore Julia Wilson round out the 10 returners. They will be fighting for minutes off the bench.

Joining the Zags are junior transfer guards Emmy Roach (Rider) and Jocelyn Medina (Denver) and freshman forward Abby Lusk, from Pocatello, Idaho. All three had solid minutes at FanFest.

“We have players who can make plays, who can make shots, who can rebound,” Fortier said. “We’re going to be able to play a lot of them and a lot of them are gonna be able to make an impact.”

With a team loaded with experience, preseason practices have allowed the Zags to pick up where they left off.

“We’re still gonna play with two forwards, we’re still gonna run the floor, we’re still gonna shoot a bunch of 3s,” Fortier said. “But within that context it does afford us an opportunity to wiggle a little bit and tinker.”

Gonzaga won’t have any difficulty scoring, and the Zags will look to push the pace whenever they can. But they must cut down on turnovers and improve defensively.

“Defensively we can be a lot better,” Turner said, pointing the finger squarely at herself.

The Zags were ranked 49th by Bart Torvik, whose analytical data is similar to the KenPom rankings in men’s basketball. No other non-Power Four school was represented in Torvik’s top 50.

Gonzaga is heavily favored to win the Pac-12 Conference in its first year in the rebuilt league.

It’s likely just the Pac-12 Tournament winner will earn a berth to the NCAA Tournament. The conference doesn’t have the credentials that the men’s teams have at this point.

The Zags don’t want to just get to the NCAA Tournament, though. They want to do something no other Gonzaga team has done – get to the Elite Eight, if not further.

“Win the conference tournament, make it to postseason and then hopefully get further than a game there this year,” Turner said.

Said Whittaker: “Everyone got a taste of what it’s like to be at the (NCAA) Tournament and everyone wants more. So it’s just elevating from what we had last year. We’ve built that foundation. No excuses. We’ve been together for a year.”

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga, even in new league, remain title favorites | Pac-12 women
Gonzaga.summary:
Pac-12 women’s basketball most likely will be divided into three tiers in the reconditioned conference.

Gonzaga and San Diego State should occupy the top two spots by season’s end.

Third through sixth – featuring Washington State, Colorado State, Oregon State and Boise State – will be highly competitive but could finish in any order.

And the three lowest places should be decided between Utah State, Fresno State and Texas State.

If Gonzaga plays as advertised, though, the Zags could make it a solo run to a conference championship, creating a fourth tier.

The Zags are expected to carry over their West Coast Conference dominance into the Pac-12.

Gonzaga is ranked No. 49 in the Bart Torvik preseason analytical data – the highest ranking for a non-Power Four conference school. Oregon State is 69th, Colorado State 80th and San Diego State 97th.

Here’s a look at the predicted order of finish:

1. Gonzaga. Easy, easy choice here.

None of the nine conference teams bring back a roster as deep as the Zags. Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who dominated in the WCC and was named the Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year last season, is expected to pick up where she left off. She’s the runaway pick as the Pac-12’s Player of the Year. Whittaker has plenty of support down low. Couple that with a perimeter that features the top 3-point shooting team in the nation a year ago and opponents will have to pick their poison in what they try to defend.

2. San Diego State. The Aztecs cruised to the Mountain West regular-season championship last year, stumbling once in 20 games. They were upset in the conference tournament, but extended their season in the WBIT where they were eliminated in the quarterfinals. SDSU has four of five starters back and add four transfers and three freshmen. The Aztecs finished 27-6 overall, tying the record for most wins in a season.

3. Oregon State. The Beavers can match up with any guards in the conference, but they sorely lack an experienced inside presence. OSU returns WCC All-Conference First Team picks Jenna Villa and Kennedie Shuler, both senior guards. Shuler was named the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and is arguably the best point guard in the conference. Villa, a transfer a year ago from Washington State, averaged 14.9 points in a breakout season.

4. Colorado State. The Rams won the MW Tournament last year, advancing to the NCAA Tournament where they showed well in a 65-62 loss to Michigan State and finished 27-8. CSU returns just one starter and bring in eight players including five transfers. The Rams have thrived in recent seasons on transfers.

5. Washington State. The Cougars have much to prove, but have a strong foundation. They return five starters – six if you count Malia Rudd, who started 20 games as a freshman. Leading the way is senior 5-8 guard Eleonora Villa, a second team All-WCC selection. The Italy native averaged a career-high 16.5 points and 3.6 assists while playing 34.8 minutes a game.

6. Boise State. The Broncos were highly competitive in the MW a year ago, finishing 25-9 overall and 14-6 in league. They must replace four starters. Coach Gordy Presnell begins his 39th season as a head coach, 21st at BSU. He’s six wins shy of 800 (794-392). The retooling will include three transfers and four freshmen.

7. Fresno State. The Bulldogs have much work ahead. They bring back one starter from a team that finished 15-18. The Bulldogs have brought in eight transfers and three freshmen. They get the nod here over Texas State based on playing in a tougher conference previously.

8. Texas State. The Bobcats have the lone new head coach in Chris Kielsmeier. He was previously a head coach at Cleveland State, Wayne State College and Howard Payne. Texas State brings back two starters. Kielsmeier signed eight transfers.

9. Utah State. The Aggies might as well be starting from rock bottom. They lost 18 straight to end last year after a 6-6 start. They return two starters, but wholesale changes are expected with six transfers.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women picked to win new Pac-12; WSU selected sixth | Notebook
Gonzaga.summary:
With five starters and five other returners, it is no surprise that the Gonzaga women’s basketball team was tapped to win the Pac-12 Conference championship in a media poll released Thursday.

The Bulldogs’ top seven scorers return from a team that finished 24-10 and won the West Coast Conference title in its final season in the league.

Oregon State was picked to finish second in the remodeled conference. The Beavers may have been picked second based on their reputation and penchant for postseason success. In the final year of the original Pac-12 (2023-24), they advanced to the Elite Eight.

San Diego State, which won the Mountain West championship last year, was picked third followed by Colorado State, Boise State, Washington State, Fresno State, Texas State and Utah State.

Gonzaga received 16 of 19 first-place votes. Oregon State received one and San Diego State received two.

Colorado State won the MWC Tournament last year and advanced to the NCAA Tournament.

WSU returns six players who started at various times. The Cougars have much to prove after stumbling to a 9-25 record last year.

ESPN released its preseason bracketology compiled by Charlie Creme on Monday. Gonzaga is picked as the automatic qualifier from the Pac-12 as a 10 seed. Oregon State and San Diego State are picked in the new 76-team field to play play-in games.

Players to watch

The Pac-12 also released its Preseason Impact List.

Gonzaga junior forward Lauren Whittaker, the WCC Player and Freshman of the Year last season, and junior guard Allie Turner, an All-WCC first-team selection a year ago, were two of 18 players named. Each school was allowed to nominate two players.

Named from WSU are seniors Alex Covill (post) and Eleonora Villa (guard), an All-WCC second-team pick last year.

Former WSU guard Jenna Villa and point guard Kennedie Shuler were selected from Oregon State. Shuler was the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and Villa was a first-team selection.

Add to the list

Gonzaga’s Whittaker was named to two more watch lists.

Whittaker, from Christchurch, New Zealand, is on the Naismith Trophy Women’s College Player of the Year preseason list along with the Katrina McClain Award preseason list. On Tuesday she was named to the Becky Hammon Mid-Major Player of the Year preseason list.

She is one of two Pac-12 players on the Hammon list.

In her first season playing for the Zags a year ago, Whittaker averaged 19.1 points and 10.2 rebounds per game with 649 points and a school-record 348 rebounds.

Coach list

Lisa Fortier, who is entering her 13th season as head coach at Gonzaga, has been named to the Kathy Delaney-Smith Coach of the Year preseason watch list.

Fortier is one of 20 coaches nationally selected to the preseason list. The award is in its fourth season.

She enters the season four wins away from becoming the all-time winningest Gonzaga coach with a 313-84 overall record. That’s a .788 winning percentage. The winningest coach is Kelly Graves (316-136, .699), who is beginning his 13th season at Oregon.

Gonzaga.title: Gonzaga women see plenty of bright spots in exhibition rout of Westmont
Gonzaga.summary:
As exhibitions go, it was true to form.

Dig deeper and it’s clear to see why there’s excitement about two teams that play in McCarthey Athletic Center.

Nearly a month to the day of its first preseason practice, the Gonzaga women’s basketball team showed it was ready to play Tuesday, cruising past the NCAA Division II Westmont College Warriors 84-43 before 4,490.

All 12 available Gonzaga players saw time in the first half, and a freshman made an emphatic debut.

Abby Lusk, the Zags’ lone freshman from Pocatello, Idaho, made the first two shots of her career, both 3-pointers, and had 10 points on 4 of 4 shooting in five minutes.

Impressive considering she had been out a week after spraining an ankle. Coach Lisa Fortier said Lusk was a game-time decision.

“It’s the little things that, like, Little Me dreamed about,” Lusk said of her debut. “Getting your first college baskets. It’s just a surreal moment. Being able to make two (back-to-back 3-pointers) is kind of fun too. Seeing the love and support from the bench and the girls on the court … it was everything I envisioned it being.”

Lusk finished with 12 points and four rebounds in 11 minutes.

“We wanted to get her under the lights and see how she did,” Fortier said. “And she did very well. … I think her parents would have come up if they would have known she was going to play. But we had no idea.”

Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who was the West Coast Conference Player and Freshman of the Year last season, scored Gonzaga’s first basket. Whittaker ate up the smaller Warriors inside in the opening 20 minutes with 16 points on 6-of-8 shooting to go with four rebounds, two assists and two steals. She finished with a game-high 24 points, six rebounds and three assists in 21 minutes.

Four of five starters from a year ago started Tuesday and Mead High graduate and junior guard Teryn Gardner stepped into the lineup, replacing fifth-year guard Ines Bettencourt.

The lone Zag not to play was sophomore forward Jaiden Haile, who was the WCC’s Sixth Woman of the Year last season. She was wearing a boot from an overuse injury. She started shooting in light practice last week.

Every Gonzaga player logged at least 10 minutes.

Another bright spot was the play of senior guard Zeryhia Aokuso. She scored from all areas, finishing with 14 points in 18 minutes.

Gonzaga asserted authority early in the third quarter, using a 7-0 spurt to set the tone. It was the most pleasing stretch for Fortier.

“The thing I liked the most was how we came out in the third,” Fortier said. “Hopefully our team is going to be a team that gets leads and then play from the front versus always coming from behind. We talked at halftime about what our energy was going to look like in the third. I thought it was really good energy, probably our best quarter.”

It was the second game in two days for Westmont, from Santa Barbara, California. The Warriors fell 71-46 at Washington State on Sunday.

Gonzaga opens the season with three straight home games, beginning Monday when North Dakota State visits. The Bison are picked to win the Summit League championship.

NDSU is similar to Gonzaga. The Bison return four of five starters including a Player of the Year and Defensive Player of the Year.

Gonzaga opened the season at NDSU last year, winning 81-66.

“North Dakota State is really good,” Fortier said. “So it’s a tough opener. Hopefully we’ll get the best work we can in the next few days.”

Oregon State.title: Oregon State's Huge Task At Boise State, and Atkinson's 2027 Commitment
Oregon State.summary:
The Oregon State Beavers are on a two-game losing streak, bringing their record to 5-4 and delaying their qualification for bowl season. This week, they face an opponent that's been circled on their calendar for quite a while: the G6 playoff frontrunner Boise State Broncos. Are they ready for the challenge?

The football program did get some great news in the last week, however: starting quarterback Braden Atkinson has committed to the Beavers for the 2027 season, following in the footsteps of star receiver Jesse Legree. 

Hear audio from JaMarcus Shephard's media availability ahead of this weekend's showdown on the blue turf as well.

All that, plus the five college football games you need to watch this weekend outside of Oregon State's matchup. Go Beavs.

Oregon State.title: No Reason To Panic About Oregon State Football's Pac-12 Hopes
Oregon State.summary:
Oregon State suffered a tough loss this past weekend against the Fresno State Bulldogs, a performance that gives this Beavers' squad some real adversity to deal with after five consecutive wins. That being said, there's still plenty left for the Beavers to accomplish this season despite now having three losses on their record.

Your host Matt Bagley gives his reaction to what went right and what went wrong for Oregon State in that game, and why there should be no reason to panic despite the mistakes of JaMarcus Shephard's team.

It's also time to look ahead to a matchup against a tricky Texas State team, who pushed Boise State to their limits. It could be a return to form for #Pac12AfterDark. Hear JaMarcus Shephard's Monday comments in the buildup to that matchup.

Meanwhile on the hardwood, Justin Joyner's men's basketball had a strong opening win against Weber State. It was an encouraging, well-rounded display with all of the Beavers' toughest obstacles still yet to come.  

All that, and the five college football games that you should watch this Saturday. Go Beavs.

Music by audionautix.com. All music produced by Jason Shaw on AudionautiX is released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Oregon State.title: Effects of Jesse Legree's Commitment To OSU + 2026 Basketball Previews
Oregon State.summary:
One of the biggest stories in college football of the last two weeks: Oregon State freshman wide receiver Jesse Legree making a formal commitment to the Beavers through the 2027-2028 season.  For a good chunk of this week's episode of State of the Beavs, we're looking at that decision and what it means for the overall growth of the program - even if JaMarcus Shephard would rather take things one game at a time. 

You'll hear clips both from Shephard's media availability coming out of the bye week, and from Legree's announcement at his high school in Baltimore before we look at the Beavers' matchup with Fresno State in California on Halloween. 

With just a few days before the start of college basketball season, it's also time to look at the Beaver men's and women's programs. John Severs and Ben Pahl were present at Oregon State's media day in Portland last week and join the show to offer their perspectives.

All that, plus the five college football games that you need to watch over Halloween weekend. Go Beavs.

Music by audionautix.com. All music produced by Jason Shaw on AudionautiX is released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Oregon State.title: Questions Following Oregon State Football's 5-2 Start To 2026
Oregon State.summary:
Oregon State are one win away from reaching bowl eligibility in JaMarcus Shephard's first season as head coach after a 48-30 victory against the Washington State Cougars. Of course, we dive into a recap of the action from that contest as Jesse Legree, AJ Newberry, and the rest of the Beavers continue to spearhead a monumental turnaround. Hear audio from Takari Hickle and Trey Glasper about that result.

However, it's also important to note that after the contest, Shephard was quick to offer condolences to the families of the victims of last weeks' tragic shooting in Bend at Silver Rail Elementary.  Hear Shephard's comments, and why they matter to the state and the college football community at-large.

After that, your host Matt Bagley dives into three questions that have arisen in our minds about the Beavers' season following the hot start.

All that, and the five college football games you should watch this week as the Beavers get a bye week to prepare for a road matchup with Fresno State to close the month of October. Go Beavs. 

Music by audionautix.com. All music produced by Jason Shaw on AudionautiX is released under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.

Oregon State.title: Jesse Legree Continues To Set Records For Oregon State Football
Oregon State.summary:
En route to a 4-2 record for Oregon State football, true freshman wide receiver Jesse Legree has been one of the most electrifying players in the country.  The Baltimore native became the first Oregon State wide receiver ever to post over 100 receiving yards in six consecutive games, something not even legendary Beavers like Brandin Cooks and Mike Hass were able to do back in their day.

This week on State of the Beavs, we react to the incredible pace that Legree has set for himself while leading the nation in both receiving yards and touchdowns. We'll also react to Oregon State's thorough beatdown of San Diego State by a score of 66-14 this past weekend, which has made fans realize JaMarcus Shephard's talk of chasing a Pac-12 title is more than simply talk.

Ahead of the Oregon State-Washington State contest this week, we'll predict how things might go against Kirby Moore's squad, and look forward to the reunion with former Beavs head coach Trent Bray.

All that, plus the five games that you need to watch in college football this weekend. Go Beavs.

Washington State.title: WSU RB rotations tilting, Kirby Moore clarifies 'good luck with that' comment and more | Notebook
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN — As Washington State barrels toward the end of coach Kirby Moore’s debut season, preparing to host San Diego State this weekend for the season finale, a few patterns are cementing themselves in the Cougars’ offense.

One of them is this: At the running back position, things are tilting the direction of Kirby Vorhees, who has earned 30-plus offensive snaps each of the last six games. Meanwhile, redshirt sophomore Maxwell Woods has seen his tally hover in the teens in the same span.

In the Cougs’ last outing, a 42-14 defeat to Texas State last weekend, Vorhees was on the field for 44 snaps, Woods for just 19. Vorhees turned in 55 yards on 12 carries, while Woods turned four carries into 24 yards.

“I think sometimes when you’re playing with tempo, the same guy at times can can be on the field there for a few more snaps. I do think we’d probably want a little bit better balance there,” Moore said. “Sometimes things are happening fast with personnels. Both of those guys made plays on on Saturday, and they’re both gonna make more plays here this week and be a part of the offensive plan.”

It’s been a topic worth monitoring in recent weeks, in large part, because the Cougars’ rushing attack is showing signs of life. Earlier this month, WSU set a program record with 535 rushing yards in a historic win over Colorado State. In that one, Vorhees and Woods each cleared the 100-yard mark, an equally monumental milestone for the tailbacks — whose rushing offense had otherwise left a lot to be desired.

Plus, in Saturday’s game, both looked sharp. Vorhees ripped off two rushes of 10-plus yards, and Woods covered 16 yards combined on his first two rushes. But as the game wore on, the Cougs’ offense was mired in mistakes and penalties, taking away opportunities for Woods and Vorhees to make their mark on the game.

Moore clarifies ‘good luck with that’ remark

After WSU’s loss to Texas State, Moore was making his opening statement when he delivered this comment: “Second drive, we get a first down. We get a penalty, first-and-20. Good luck with that.”

On the play in question, WSU left tackle Jaylin Caldwell was whistled for holding on a second-down play, wiping away a 17-yard completion from quarterback Owen Eshelman to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy. That set the Cougars back to second-and-20, and three plays later, punter Max Dean’s kick was blocked.

The comment made waves among WSU fans, who were concerned that Moore didn’t appear to have confidence in his team digging itself out of a hole.

“I think I misspoke on that,” Moore said on Monday. “It was second-and-10, and I think we had the completion there on the the bigger intermediate, so it was second-and-20. I think anywhere in college football, second-and-20, the percentages are in the defense’s favor, and so there’s just naturally some challenges with that in terms of creating chunk plays.

“I’ve got a ton of confidence in our guys, their energy and effort. Obviously, there was execution flaws there on Saturday. Some of those, you gotta give Texas State credit, and then some of those were self-inflicted for sure, whether it was earlier, when it was when we’re crossing the 50 and we shot ourselves in the foot, and then you get behind the sticks.”

Moore finding his groove in game management

As he wraps up his first year as a head coach, Moore is still finding his footing in the game management department, still trying to find a balance between going for it at the end of halves or playing it safe.

“I think naturally, when the head coach is involved in one side of the ball a little bit more, the coordinators are are naturally able to call timeouts,” Moore said. “So if there’s something specifically that Coach (Trent) Bray or Coach (Derek) Sage need a certain look, tey’re able to call timeouts. That’s been a change.

“From a clock standpoint, there’s the book, and we have some people within the football program who are upstairs, keeping track of when we should be calling timeouts. When we might have two downs from an offensive standpoint, or being ready defensively for someone to have two downs. So there’s a lot of communication, whether it’s the people upstairs or with the coordinators on the field.”

Washington State.title: WSU ready to host San Diego State for flex game, season finale | First look
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Here is a first look at Washington State’s home game against San Diego State on Saturday afternoon.

What is it?

To cap off the season, WSU will host San Diego State for the teams’ flex matchup, an invention of the Pac-12 to position its best team with the best chance to make the College Football Playoff. It’s the regular-season finale for the Cougars, who will miss a bowl game for just the second time in the last 11 full seasons, while the Aztecs have already punched their ticket to the following week’s Pac-12 championship game – plus a bowl game.

It will be the second meeting of the season between WSU and San Diego State. The Aztecs handed the Cougars a 26-20 road loss in San Diego on Oct. 31.

WSU will honor 14 seniors before the game, including linebacker Keith Brown, receivers Daniel Blood and Darrius Clemons, defensive end Linus Zunk, cornerback Jalil Tucker, offensive linemen Jonny Lester and Jaylin Caldwell and others.

Where is it?

Gesa Field at Martin Stadium in Pullman.

When is it?

Kickoff is set for 3:30 p.m.

Where can I watch it?

The CW will broadcast the game.

Who is favored?

SDSU opened as a 2-point favorite.

How did the Cougars fare last week?

WSU is coming off a 42-14 road loss to Texas State in San Marcos, where the Cougars took an early 7-0 lead before letting the Bobcats follow with six unanswered touchdowns, turning things into a blowout. WSU had two kicks blocked, one punt and one field goal, and the Cougs were hit with seven costly penalties for 45 yards.

It was a mistake-ridden outing for WSU, whose defense was no match for Texas State’s high-flying offense. The Bobcats piled up 299 rushing yards, including 146 from running back Torrence Burgess Jr. and 127 from quarterback Brad Jackson, who scored three touchdowns on the ground and one through the air. Texas State tallied nine rushing plays of 10-plus yards and four passing plays of 15-plus yards.

For WSU, the most consequential penalty belonged to receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy. On fourth-and-3 from the Texas State 37, WSU was lined up to go for it. But Ganashamoorthy jumped early, turning that play into a fourth-and-8, forcing punter Max Dean to come out and boot it away. Later in the Bobcats’ ensuing drive, they punched it in for six, taking a 21-7 lead.

Plus, in the third quarter, the Cougars (2-9, 1-6 Pac-12) were whistled for back-to-back false starts, one on Caldwell and one on tight end Jack Pedersen. That proved to be too much for WSU, whose margin for error has been razor-thin this season.

Headed into this one, a big question hovered over the entire operation: Could WSU look more like the team that hung 73 points on Colorado State the week prior, or would the Cougars look like the team that had lost six straight games prior? After the first few minutes, it looked like the former would take place, but it didn’t take long for the latter to surface once again.

Scouting San Diego State…

Since earning a victory over WSU in late October, San Diego State has followed with two more wins, a 30-13 home triumph over Utah State and a 22-20 stunner against Boise State over the weekend, shaking up the conference championship picture. With that win, the Aztecs earned themselves another crack at the Broncos in the Pac-12 title game on Dec. 4.

San Diego State (6-5, 5-2) doesn’t have as much to play for in Saturday’s game against WSU. How motivated will the Aztecs be? Will they consider resting key players? It’s possible this weekend’s game doesn’t have the same tenor as a typical regular-season game, in large part because it isn’t.

To engineer a shocking win over first-place Boise State last weekend, SDSU redshirt freshman quarterback Stone Saunders laced a touchdown pass to receiver Jaylon Hawkins, who made an acrobatic catch in the end zone. That brought the Aztecs within one, 20-19, with a hair under two minutes to play. The visitors couldn’t tack on the 2-point conversion.

When the Broncos got the ball back, they went for it on fourth-and-3 at the SDSU 45-yard line, a coaching decision widely criticized around the country. Boise State couldn’t convert, and when SDSU took over on downs, it ended a clutch drive with a game-winning field goal from Cooper DiLeva as the clock hit zeroes.

The Aztecs have leaned on their rushing attack to win their past two games, totaling 179 yards against Boise State and 210 against Utah State the week prior. The tip of the spear has been tailback Javion Kinnard: 113 yards to beat the Aggies and 86 more to top the Broncos. Usually a pocket passer, Saunders has also been using his legs more, churning out 41 yards and a touchdown in Boise.

On the year, San Diego State is still allowing an average of 31.1 points per game and 425 yards per game, both of which rank in the No. 120s of 138 FBS teams. But the Aztecs have looked like a different team in their last few games, and they’ve made sharp improvements on the defensive end.

What happened last time?

In SDSU’s 26-20 win over WSU earlier this year, the Aztecs opened up a two-score lead early in the fourth quarter, and the Cougs’ sputtering offense couldn’t find a spark. They later scored, getting a rushing touchdown from QB Owen Eshelman, but with a chance to tie the game late in the fourth frame, the visitors’ comeback sputtered out with a turnover on downs.

Washington State.title: Cougars Open Scoring Before Texas State Pulls Away
3 thoughts, and a bonus reflection, from WSU's loss to Texas State | Rewind
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Linus Zunk took a deep breath and stared straight ahead, taking in the question and trying to find a response.

When the season is over next week, what do you think you’ll miss most about playing with this group of guys?

Only a few minutes had passed since the buzzer ran out on Washington State’s latest loss, a 42-14 road defeat Saturday evening at Texas State, and the senior defensive end had only one more game in his college career. He will play his final college snaps next week in Pullman, wrapping up his first and only season at WSU.

So with that looming, Zunk had to take in the gravity of the moment, of the fact that the end of his collegiate career was closing in quicker than he had realized. He took his time with his answer, even at one point apologizing for the pause.

Then he found the words he was looking for.

“I’m just gonna miss being able to look to my right and to my left,” Zunk said, “and seeing a bunch of guys that are hungry to work and that I know care as much as I do. We say it all the time, even though it really doesn’t have to be said, but everybody gives their all for each other, and I’m gonna miss that.

“I know that these guys care, and it hurts me that the team hasn’t seen the results maybe of the work they’ve put in, but that’s, I mean, that’s life, right? So yeah, I’m just gonna miss the guys, really. You can talk football all you want but we have some great people in the room. We have some great people in the building.”

A Vanderbilt transfer, Zunk has played an invaluable role on this WSU defense, turning in oodles of quarterback pressures. He’ll be remembered fondly on this 2026 Cougar defense.

His story is worth telling for lots of reasons, but after Saturday’s game, this one felt most prominent: The Cougars were only able to get a handful of pressures. That’s where this edition of the WSU rewind starts.

1. WSU’s pass rush was largely ineffective

All told, WSU generated only three pressures on Texas State quarterback Brad Jackson, according to Pro Football Focus: one apiece from rotation defensive lineman Josh Wedel, linebacker Isaiah Hung and defensive lineman Kaden Beatty. It was the Cougars’ fewest all season.

That means WSU’s two starting defensive ends, Zunk and Matyus McLain, didn’t get any pressures on Jackson. That was problematic for the Cougs’ defense, which yielded several chunk plays, including several through the air: a 21-yard pass to Zecharaiah Sample, a 21-yard connection to Chris Dawn Jr. and a 15-yard touchdown pass from Jackson to Beau Sparks.

Context is key. The Bobcats were clearly making an effort to get the ball out quickly, likely in an effort to neutralize Zunk and McLain, who have racked up tons of pressure this fall. In that way, there wasn’t much they could do on an individual level. But defensive coordinator Trent Bray and his players couldn’t scheme around that, and Texas State took advantage.

It’s a compliment to Zunk and McLain, who have played well enough to command that type of attention. But it also means that if the Cougars want to end their season on a high note and take down San Diego State in next weekend’s season finale, they’ll need to get more pressure on Aztec QB Stone Saunders.

2. Where did the run go?

In the opening minutes of this one, judging by the way running back Kirby Vorhees and quarterback Owen Eshelman were playing, you might have thought Colorado State defenders were still out there, just wearing Texas State jerseys. On their opening drive, the Cougs ran the ball effectively and compellingly, needing only five plays to reach the end zone.

For the game, Vorhees totaled 55 yards on 12 carries, and fellow tailback Maxwell Woods added 24 yards on four carries. That adds up to 16 carries for 79 yards, an average rush of nearly 5 yards. Those two had few issues getting downhill, at least in the first half.

But considering the way they were carrying the ball, it was curious to see their opportunities reduce on some level in the second half. On one drive early in the third quarter, Vorhees turned in rushes of 16, 8, 5 and 0 yards. He got only three more carries the rest of the game.

Woods’ first carry was an 11-yard gash midway through the second quarter. He slipped free for an extra 5 yards later in the drive. Across the remainder of the game, he saw only two more carries.

This context is also important: WSU’s offensive line was having real trouble giving Eshelman time to pass. That seemed to be the reason why almost all of his throws were quick-outs. He didn’t have a particularly accurate game, either, missing a few throws he usually connects on. If that was such a problem, why not turn things over to your running backs, who had been playing so well?

“The box tells you, you should be able to run the ball a number of times versus these guys,” coach Kirby Moore said, “and so they put you in that position to have opportunities to run the ball. We just unfortunately, from an offensive standpoint, didn’t finish there on drives.”

3. The Cougars can’t keep allowing so many big plays on defense

Sometimes the most important conclusions are the easiest to notice: WSU keeps permitting too many big plays.

In Saturday’s game, the Cougs were dinged for nine rushes of 10-plus yards, including a 44-yard touchdown rush from Jackson, another 36-yard keeper from Jackson for six, plus a 40-yard rush from running back Torrence Burgess Jr. and a 34-yard rush from Jackson. The Bobcats have one of the country’s most explosive offenses, sure, but the Cougs were making it too easy.

Consider this pattern: On the year, the Cougars have allowed 84 big plays, which are defined as rushes of 10-plus yards and passes of 20-plus yards. That number ranks No. 102 in the country, including second-to-last in the Pac-12. In the conference, the only team worse is Colorado State – the same group that allowed the once-hapless Cougar offense to drop 73 points.

BONUS: Kirby Moore seemed quick to doubt his offense

After the game, in his opening statement to begin his postgame news conference, Moore said this: “Second drive, we get a first down. We get a penalty, first-and-20. Good luck with that.”

In context, Moore was talking about the way penalties hampered his team’s offense, to the tune of seven for 45 yards. They were a killer all game for the Cougars, who committed back-to-back false starts at one point in there. There’s no denying the impact of penalties in this one.

But when he says “good luck with that,” Moore seems to imply that his Cougars can’t dig themselves out of a hole created by penalties. In the end, it turned out to be true, but it likely doesn’t imbue WSU’s locker room with confidence.

That’s what a lot of coaching is: giving your guys confidence, regardless of how realistic it should be.

In the past, Moore has been careful to protect his players with the words he chooses, including refusing to single out quarterback Caden Pinnick in the height of his struggles. But other times, like after Saturday’s game, his tune has seemed to change a bit.

Washington State.title: 'A guy we gotta build this thing around': In WSU's loss to Texas State, LB Isaiah Hung shines with TD
Washington State.summary:
SAN MARCOS, Texas — At some point earlier this fall, in a sea of purple and white, Isaiah Hung felt his confidence soar. Hung and his Washington State teammates were locked in a road game at Kansas State, part of the two-loss skid with which the Cougars opened the season, but good luck blaming Hung.

In that game, a blowout loss for WSU, Hung registered a team-best eight tackles. He registered seven of the solo variety. He didn’t miss a single tackle, and he earned a Pro Football Focus defensive grade of 84.1, the top grade in that entire game.

“I feel like that was probably the game that gave me my confidence,” Hung said, “and told me, hey, I can really do this.’”

More than two months later, Hung is still playing like it, most recently in WSU’s 42-14 loss to Texas State. In the final moments of the Cougars’ second-to-last game of the season, Hung pounced on a fumble and returned it 30 yards for a touchdown, which he says was his first since playing youth football growing up in the Kansas City area.

In this one, Hung tallied seven tackles, including five solo. He picked up one tackle for loss, and he turned in one quarterback hurry. He was all over the field, in other words, the same way he has been for just about the entire season.

“I was really just tracking the running back,” Hung said of his touchdown, “and Jaylen (Thomas) came and fit him up good, popped him, and I just got a hand in there, pulled the ball out, and ball’s on the ground. My eyes got really wide, and I felt like I was dragging a trailer running to the end zone. But I made it. Guys picked up some blocks for me, so it was cool.”

In the grand scheme of things, Hung’s touchdown might get lost in the shuffle. The Cougars are now 2-9 on the season, including just 1-6 in Pac-12 play. Their season has been rotten, and while their defense has had plenty of moments to remember, they’ve slogged through lots to forget, too. Those who care about WSU football and invest in its success are probably itching for this season to just end already.

What nobody will be able to forget, though, is Hung. In many ways, his outing in Saturday’s game was a microcosm of his season: He was a constant on the field, in many of the biggest plays the Cougars made on defense. He was reliable as ever, and with his touchdown, he showed he has a nose for the big plays, too.

“It was for sure a cool moment. First college forced fumble recovery and touchdown,” said Hung, who added that his parents were in the stands to watch him play. “But I mean, there’s a bigger picture in the game and there’s a lot of drives that could have ended differently if we would have all been on our work. So really, it’s just another play, and we gotta execute better throughout the rest of the game.”

If it’s possible to get a window into Hung’s brain and how it works, that sentence might be it. In order to ascend this season, going from relatively unknown piece to one of the top three players on this Washington State defense, he had a burning desire to improve, and he hasn’t been shy about when he’s needed to be better. After Saturday’s game, he said he “had a few big mistakes.”

“I’m gonna come back next week. I’m gonna push myself throughout the week,” Hung said, “and push my teammates to be better, so we can execute every time we need to.”

What mistakes did he feel like he made?

“Just execution,” Hung said. “Obviously, you’re gonna make mistakes. Things are gonna happen. It’s football. But it’s really how you respond and how you come back from that mistake. And I feel like sometimes I get caught up in my head, and I feel like that’s still something I can work on, building my confidence up throughout. We only have one week left, so finishing the rest of the season, finish strong, and really just play for my brothers.”

“I love Isaiah Hung,” WSU coach Kirby Moore added. “He’s a huge part of the future here moving forward at Washington State. He competes his tail off in academics, on the field, in the weight room. He’s a guy we gotta build this thing around.”

Next weekend, after the Cougars’ final game of the season, their offseason will arrive. There will be a pecking order of players that Moore and coaches prioritize retaining. In that way, it’s no surprise that Moore referenced building things around Hung.

He’s that good, and he’ll only keep getting better. If the Cougars play their cards right, he’ll be doing so in a crimson uniform next fall.

Washington State.title: Washington State fought to rebuild a conference it can't compete in | Jacob Thorpe
Washington State.summary:
For three years, Washington State worked to rebuild the Pac-12. On Saturday, the last school invited to join the new conference showed the Cougars just how far they are from competing in it.

WSU’s tradition, history, and power conference trophy case gave them no advantages on Saturday in San Marcos against a Texas State team that is likely to compete with Boise State for the new conference’s first championship. Despite not being included in the original rebuilding plan, the Bobcats made it clear the Pac-12 belongs to its victors, not its founders.

The mirage of last week’s 73-point evisceration of Colorado State lasted through WSU’s first drive, a five-play cruise ending with an impressive, contested catch-and-run to the end zone by Daniel Blood. Afterward, WSU reverted to its typical inability to produce points against legitimate opponents.

While WSU’s offense has clearly improved a bit since making the switch to Owen Eshelman at quarterback, too often the Cougars still can’t get out of their own way, as seen with multiple false start penalties before key downs in the first half alone.

In some ways, the Cougars are a victim of inevitable regression and bad timing. In the early years of Pac-12 instability WSU had a future NFL No. 1 overall pick at quarterback in Cam Ward, followed by John Mateer, a one-time Heisman hopeful whose star has dimmed a bit at Oklahoma.

The coach, Jake Dickert, has Wake Forest ranked No. 10, tied for its highest AP ranking ever and poised to break a record when the new rankings come out next week.

The Cougars were buoyed by some superlative talent at coach and quarterback, and a fall was inevitable. That it is happening now, in the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12, is in large part bad luck and hey, maybe it was worth it to have some good seasons while trying to sell the other schools on forming a new league.

But this is brutal. WSU is emphatically positioning itself at the bottom of its own conference, and it is going to be a tough climb. The uncomfortable reality is WSU, once a proud Power Five program, will have to establish itself all over again in a diminished conference that it helped build.

New coach Kirby Moore gets a failing grade in his first season at the helm. His next test will be significantly improving the roster in the offseason. It will be eyebrow-raising if there aren’t some changes to the coaching staff, as well.

The question that has followed the Cougars all season: Does this team have an identity worth building around? Forget the record for a second. What is this team, and where is it going?

To upgrade, Moore is going to have to sell players (and coaches) on a vision of success that requires some squinting. It’s a pitch that felt more valid after the stunning eruption of offense last week, and one that lost credibility with Saturday’s 42-14 loss in San Marcos.

Four years ago, as the Pac-12’s moneymakers fled conferences with little to no regional affiliation, it felt like everything was collapsing on the Cougars. That was a bad time, and WSU made it through as well as could have been hoped.

The Cougars won the fight to preserve their conference. Now they must avoid becoming an afterthought in it.

Washington State.title: Texas State rolls over Washington State 42-14 | Recap and highlights
Washington State.summary:
SAN MARCOS, Texas — As the sun descended over UFCU Stadium, where Washington State was squaring off with Texas State for its final road game of a forgettable season, the clouds began to part a bit for the visitors.

An official emerged from a replay and announced to the crowd: Moments prior, when WSU receiver Daniel Blood had stretched for the end zone and ruled short, they had made a mistake. Blood had actually crossed the plane. Instead, a touchdown for the Cougars, who took an early lead.

For a moment, WSU looked like the team that hung a historic 73 points last week, a refreshed bunch ready to turn in a memorable final two games of the season. Instead, in a 42-14 loss to the Bobcats, the Cougars looked more like the one that had lost six straight games prior: committing a series of costly penalties, missing tackles in the middle of the field and watching their special teams look anything but special.

In their penultimate game of coach Kirby Moore’s debut season, WSU allowed Texas State to run off six unanswered touchdowns, turning a close game into a blowout by the third quarter. Quarterback Owen Eshelman completed 21 of 33 passes for 150 yards for the Cougars, who were called for seven penalties for 45 yards, including a delay of game coming out of halftime and back-to-back false starts in the third frame.

More importantly, WSU’s special teams turned in a poor day, getting two kicks blocked. In the first quarter, kicker Jack Stevens had a field goal try blocked, the third time the Cougars have had that happen this season. And later in the first frame, punter Max Dean had his kick blocked, leading to a Bobcat touchdown three plays later. With that score, Texas State took a 14-7 lead.

From there, there was little drama in this one, in large part because the Cougars couldn’t generate enough stops on defense. The Bobcats extended their lead to three scores in the second frame, when quarterback Brad Jackson sprinted untouched 44 yards to the end zone, and they made it four scores late in the third quarter, when running back Torrance Burgess Jr. capped a long drive with a short scoring plunge.

Here’s the damage that Jackson and Burgess dealt to the WSU defense: Jackson completed 11 of 119 passes for 122 yards and one touchdown, including 127 rushing yards for three scores scores, and Burgess added 146 yards and one touchdown. That helped the Bobcats pile up 299 rushing yards. On too many occasions, Cougar defenders took bad angles or missed tackles entirely, allowing the country’s second-ranked offense to treat them the way the Bobcats have to just about all their opponents.

All told, it was a game replete with mistakes from the Cougs, who absorbed too many self-inflicted errors. Early in the first half, facing a fourth-and-medium in Texas State territory, WSU receiver Branden Ganashamoorthy jumped too early. False start. The Cougars punted it away, and the Bobcats made them pay with Jackson’s first long touchdown rush.

Then late in the second quarter, when WSU got the ball back at its own 33 with a little more than one minute to play, disaster struck again. Tight end Trey Leckner took off way early, a clear false start. Moore was forced to call a timeout to prevent a 10-second runoff, and the Cougars went quietly into halftime, eschewing a chance to add points.

It wasn’t a particularly memorable game from Eshelman, who misfired on several throws over the middle of the field, a consequential development for Washington State. Headed into this one, Texas State harbored the nation’s second-worst passing defense, yielding an average of 288 yards per game. But the Cougs couldn’t take advantage, at least in part because their offensive line couldn’t give Eshelman enough time to drop back and pass.

In the final moments of the game, WSU tacked on a touchdown from linebacker Isaiah Hung on a play dripping with symbolic importance for the Cougars. WSU safety Jaylen Thomas laid a hit on Texas State running back Jaylen Jenkins — a former Cougar tailback — and forced a fumble. Hung scooped it up and returned it 30 yards for a touchdown, the first of his college career.

WSU’s offseason starts next weekend, after its final game of the year, a FLEX matchup against an opponent yet to be determined. After that, Hung might be one of the first players Moore and coaches prioritize retaining, and considering his season and potential, it’s not a bad idea. In his redshirt freshman season, Hung has registered 43 tackles, two for loss, and he’s also broken up two passes.

Hung can now add a fumble return for touchdown to his resume. That might prompt other schools to come knocking when the season ends. If the Cougars end the year with a win next weekend, no matter who their opponent is, they might be able to convince Hung to stay — and several others with promising futures.

Washington State’s defense will face its stiffest test since Oct. 24 against Boise State. 

Texas State ranks second nationally with a third-down conversion percentage of nearly 55%. The Bobcats converted 8 of 14 chances in their last game, a win over Fresno State, and they moved the sticks on 10 of 15 opportunities the week prior in a victory over Oregon State.

Washington State.title: Washington State gives No. 5 Duke a scare
Washington State.summary:
PALM DESERT, Calif. – It was a spirited effort against tall odds for Washington State.

The Cougars, facing blue-blood Duke for the first time, fell into a 19-point hole early in the second half. WSU surged back, trimming the deficit to two points in the final 30 seconds. But the fifth-ranked Blue Devils held on, sweating out a 78-74 win over the Cougs late Saturday night at Acrisure Arena.

WSU (2-4) entered the game as a 25.5-point underdog, and it seemed the oddsmakers may have called it correctly when Duke (4-2) opened a double-digit lead midway through the first half. But the Cougars didn’t let it get out of hand, staying within 13 points at the half.

The Blue Devils opened the second period with back-to-back 3-pointers and went ahead by a game-high 19 points. The Cougars answered with a pair of 3s from guard Lazerek Houston and forward Ladji Dembele. That was the story of the second half – just when it seemed Duke was going to finally put WSU away, the Cougars made key stops and hit clutch baskets to stay in it.

Eventually, WSU captured the momentum and made a legitimate push for its first lead. Ronnie Harrison scored a double-clutch layup off a fastbreak and Houston connected on a contested 3 to cap an 11-3 run over two minutes that closed the gap to 71-68.

The Blue Devils settled things down, drawing fouls in the paint and knocking down free throws to reextend the lead to seven points with 2:18 on the clock. But Harrison drilled a spot-up 3 on the ensuing possession.

The Cougs got a stop on the other end, but couldn’t score on a couple of second-chance attempts, and Duke went up by five points on a foul shot with 39 seconds left. WSU’s Jamari Phillips then hit the shot of the night, pulling up from several feet behind the 3-point line and draining it to cut the deficit to 76-74. But in a foul-heavy game, the Cougars couldn’t avoid sending Duke to the line. Star Blue Devils big man Patrick Ngongba II hit a pair of foul shots with 18 seconds left, and the Cougars couldn’t find the net on their last two possessions.

WSU’s defense, which has drawn a fair share of criticism, had a commendable performance. The Cougars defended the perimeter well, pressured the ball and consistently made the Blue Devils work for open shots. Duke shot 40.7% from the field and just 6 of 22 (27.3%) from 3-point range while committing 16 turnovers.

WSU shot 38.7% from the floor and 8 of 30 (26.7%) from beyond the arc. The Cougars lost only 10 turnovers.

The teams combined to attempt 60 free throws (51 fouls were called). Duke gained an edge at the line, going 28 of 36 on foul shots compared to an 18-for-24 mark for WSU.

Houston and guard Jaylen Harrell paced WSU with 15 points apiece. Harrell had 10 in the first half and Houston scored 10 in the second. Dembele added 12 points.

Ngongba, an NBA draft prospect and one of the nation’s best post players, led Duke with 24 points and nine rebounds. He shot 10 of 12 from the foul line. Forward Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje contributed 16 points and guard Dame Sarr, another NBA prospect, tallied 14.

Up next, the Cougars host Sam Houston at 6 p.m. Tuesday.
