Washington State.title: 'This is unacceptable': WSU falls to Duquesne in final moments, 72-71, opening season with three straight losses
Washington State.summary:
Over the weekend, after his Washington State group dropped a close road loss, David Riley went on the radio and succinctly diagnosed one of his team’s problems.

“We gotta have more leadership than that,” Riley said.

He was describing a technical foul that went against the Cougars, who proceeded to lose all momentum, winding up with a narrow loss to High Point and opening their season with two straight losses. In the aftermath of that one, it became clear that to turn things around, WSU would need to improve at responding to adversity.

After Washington State’s latest outing, a 72-71 road loss to Duquesne on Tuesday evening, it appears that much is still a work in progress. After leading for nearly 90% of game, the Cougs gave up the lead in the final seconds on an and-one, and on the other end, they couldn’t win the game as guard Lazerek Houston’s floater missed.

“It’s frustrating because there is a clear progression with our team,” said Riley, whose team allowed Duquesne to shoot 52% from the field in the second half. “We are getting better, but this is unacceptable for us to be losing these kinds of games where we control the whole game.”

WSU, which has now started a season with three straight losses for the first time since 1964, will regret this one in large part because of how much it controlled the game. The Cougs led for a total of 34 minutes, 38 seconds, leading by as many as 11. After retaking the lead midway through the first half on a 3-pointer from Tyler Kropp, who scored 10 points to get on the board for the first time all season, the Cougars didn’t lose the lead again until the final sequence.

That went like this: With about 30 seconds left, the Cougs got an acrobatic finish in traffic from guard Sebastian Akins, who totaled nine points. On the other end, Duquesne forward Kerem Konan drove at WSU freshman forward Mohamed Sankhe, who tried to draw a charge. He was called for a block. Konan completed the and-one at the free-throw line, pushing the Dukes ahead 72-71 with 12 seconds left.

But at that point, Duquesne had only been called for four team fouls in the second half, meaning they had two to give before WSU reached the bonus. So when the Cougars got the ball back, by the time the Dukes had committed two fouls, the visitors only had about five seconds to work with. Out of a timeout, WSU got the ball to Houston, who made a move into the paint but couldn’t finish a tough running floater, drifting to the side.

It was a winnable game for WSU, which had three double-digit scorers: Redshirt freshman wing Jaylen Harrell scored 19 points, Houston tallied 12 and Kropp registered 10. But many of the Cougars’ problems in this loss had more to do with two other categories: fouling and rebounds.

In the second half, WSU was whistled for 14 fouls. That resulted in a deluge of free throws for Duquesne, which converted 15 of 19 chances. Also in the second half, the Cougars gave up seven offensive rebounds, which turned into 11 second-chance points for the Dukes.

Another trend went Duquesne’s way in the second period. WSU lost only five turnovers in the first half, doing well to veer away from one of the most consistent problems the Cougars have faced in Riley’s tenure, which is now in its third year. But in the second stanza, the Cougs coughed it up nine times, leading to 14 points off turnovers.

“That second half, we got away from playing our identity, and I think it’s really obvious when you look at the stats,” Riley said in a postgame radio interview. “They had 40 points in the paint, and we had nine turnovers in the second half. Those two things are gonna kill you every time, especially on the road. We let those turnovers lead to transition points.”

Also complicating things for WSU was an injury to transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, who missed the first two games of the season with a turned ankle he suffered hours before his team’s season opener last week. He made his season debut on Tuesday, starting and playing 22 minutes, but his outing was cut short with about 3½ minutes to play, when he appeared to injure his ankle again.

It was a costly blow for the Cougs, who had gotten six points and five rebounds from Harrison, a do-it-all wing whose athleticism makes a difference on the glass and on defense. When Harrison went down, WSU subbed in transfer big man Ladji Dembele, who has put up these numbers in three games: seven points on 3-for-12 shooting, including 1-for-6 from deep, 11 rebounds, 10 fouls, five turnovers, one block and two steals.

On the year, WSU is now allowing opponents an effective field -goal percentage of 63%, which ranks No. 347 out of 362 Division I teams. The Cougars are also permitting a 2-point shooting percentage of 65%, which is No. 336. Their defensive problems have surfaced most in the second halves. Here are their opponents’ shooting percentages in the second period this season.

• Davidson: 63%

• High Point: 68%

• Duquesne: 52%

Can the Cougars turn that around? They’ll have a chance to earn their first win this weekend, hosting Division II Northwest at 10 a.m. Saturday. After that, they face a neutral-site game against Hawaii, which will provide an opportunity for these Cougars to prove that Riley is right – that they are progressing.

“We’re figuring out who we can trust out there,” Riley said, “and absolutely, we gotta start shorting that (rotation) a little bit too.”Greg Woods can be reached at 509-459-5587 or at gregw@spokesman.com.

Washington State.title: Washington State women's basketball team erupts in second quarter, then stumbles after halftime in loss at Oregon
Washington State.summary:
EUGENE – The Washington State women’s basketball team piled up 28 points during a sparkling second quarter and took a 14-point lead into halftime against the Oregon Ducks. The rest of the game was much less ideal for the Cougars.

WSU lost its rhythm after halftime and stumbled to a 64-57 nonconference loss to Oregon on Friday night at Matthew Knight Arena.

The Cougars (0-2) managed just 21 points in the second half.

WSU outscored the Ducks 28-9 in the second quarter, shooting 60% from the field in the period while limiting the Ducks to 17.6% to build a 36-22 halftime lead.

Oregon (2-0) responded with a 24-11 third quarter and swiped the lead early in the fourth. The Ducks outscored WSU 42-21 after halftime. The Cougs shot 9 of 28 from the field in the second half compared to UO’s 16-for-30 mark (6 of 10 on 3s).

Standout guard Eleonora Villa was WSU’s lone double-figure scorer with 22 points on 6 of 12 shooting. All-Big Ten guard Katie Fiso paced Oregon with 19 points.

WSU finished 36.8% from the field and 4 of 25 (16%) on 3-pointers. Oregon shot 38.7% overall and 8 of 19 (42.1%) from 3-point distance.

Washington State.title: Washington State women's basketball team opens season with big loss at Cal
Washington State.summary:
BERKELEY, Calif. – The Washington State women fell behind by double digits in the second quarter and absorbed a big loss in a nonconference season opener between former Pac-12 foes.

The California Golden Bears started to separate just before halftime and pulled away for an 80-58 win over the Cougars on Monday night at Haas Pavilion.

All-ACC Cal guard Lulu Twidale hit six 3-pointers, including a buzzer-beater at the end of the second quarter, and finished with 26 points. WSU was led by standout guard Eleonora Villa, who tallied 20 points and seven assists.

WSU trimmed the deficit to eight points midway through the third quarter, but Cal responded with a 12-2 run.

Washington State.title: WSU opens season with 76-61 loss to Davidson, dropping season-opener for second straight year
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – These days, college basketball seasons always arrive with an alluring sense of promise. The slate is clean, the roster is new, and the coach talks about how much he learned from last year and how different things will be in this one.

At Washington State, these last two years have started like that. Coach David Riley has talked with optimism about what he learned from his first season, then his second. He’s felt better about each roster he’s had, he says. Each October, he’s vowed to play better defense and scale back the turnovers.

But the Cougars have not delivered on that kind of potential. Last fall, they opened their season with a home loss to Idaho. And here on Monday night, they began Riley’s third season with a home setback to Davidson, walking off the floor as the buzzer rang on a 76-61 defeat.

“This has been the case ever since I’ve been a coach,” Riley said. “You work on things throughout the fall, throughout the summer, you build an identity, then you go to that first exhibition game, the first scrimmage or whatever, and that goes out the window. These guys kind of forget, they lose their mind. You kind of shore it up. You get to the real games. Same thing happens. And I thought this is a great example of that.”

This was about as inauspicious as it gets for the Cougars, who shot just 35% from the floor, including 5 for 24 from beyond the arc. Trailing by as many as 19, WSU allowed Davidson to convert 55% of field goals, including 63% in the second half. Offense was a mud slog for the Cougars. It was like a hot knife through butter for the Wildcats, who sank 12 of their 23 tries from distance, six from returning starting guard Sam Brown.

Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell scored a team-best 13 points for WSU, which used a 10-0 run to make things interesting in the second half, drawing within 47-38. But the Wildcats followed by getting three straight layups, stretching their lead back out to double digits, where it stayed for the remainder of the game.

On offense, the Cougs got lots of good looks. They just couldn’t knock them down. After the game, Riley said this is “one of the best shooting teams I’ve coached,” but it didn’t show: Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips connected on just 2 of 9 shots from deep, Harrell and Wake Forest transfer Sebastian Akins went 1-for-3 and UNLV transfer big man Ladji Dembele misfired on all three he tried. TCU transfer guard RJ Jones also went 0-for-2.

What’s behind those misses? Riley diagnosed the problem by pointing to the way his group couldn’t flow from its first look to an alternative one – the second action, he likes to call them. That was a problem last year’s team dealt with. One game into this season, these Cougars appear to have the same issue.

“It’s like right now in the offense, we freeze up after that first action, and all of a sudden we don’t know where those shots are coming from,” Riley said. “It’s hard to have confidence in those shots. You kinda get a random look, and you’re not ready for it, and I think some of that is just confidence. It’s hard to win when one team shoots 52% from three, and we shot 20.”

WSU played this game without East Texas A&M transfer Ronnie Harrison, who turned his ankle during pregame shootaround, Riley said. Harrison logged a double-double with 23 points and 11 rebounds in the Cougars’ exhibition win over Washington last week, and with his do-it-all skillset, he figures to play a central role on this team. Listed at 6-foot-8 and 228 pounds, Harrison is a senior and a compelling athlete, making his absence a big one for his group.

Riley hopes Harrison can play in WSU’s next game, a road test against High Point on Saturday, but he isn’t sure because the injury happened so soon before Monday’s game. If he’s out again, it’s a serious development for the Cougs, who need his shot-creation abilities and his veteran presence. It’s hard to overstate how big a loss Harrison’s is.

But on Monday, would he have turned a loss into a win? It’s hard to say. The Cougars looked disjointed on both sides of the ball. They gave up too many open triples to the Wildcats, who made offense look easy. Then they missed too many of those looks on offense. WSU has 14 newcomers, which Riley talked about after the game, and it’s not easy jelling that many players into a read-and-react system like Riley’s.

“It was clear we were on our heels a little bit all game,” Riley said. “It looked like a team with a bunch of newcomers playing a team with three returning starters that kinda knew what’s what.”

After the game, Harrell attributed part of this loss to effort, saying, “I feel like our effort wasn’t the way it was…. We practice hard every day. Since the summertime, we’ve been going at each other. We know what it takes to win, and I feel like today we didn’t show what we really had. That wasn’t the team that I play with all year. So we’re gonna get it right.”

That’s certainly not where the Cougars want to be after Game 1, talking about effort. Riley was relayed Harrell’s comments. Did he agree?

“It’s hard to think and play at the same time,” Riley said, “and I think that these guys want to go out there and compete. But when they’re thinking and they’re timid out there because they’re thinking, it looks the way it did.”

WSU has lots of time to turn this around, to make a second-straight season-opening home loss look like an exception to the rule. But it’s not a particularly encouraging start to the season for the Cougars, who now get a road game against a High Point team that won 31 games and made the NCAA Tournament second round last year.

Washington State.title: WSU hoops ready to kick off new season with home matchup against Davidson
Washington State.summary:
Earlier this summer, when David Riley was enjoying a break from coaching the Washington State’s men’s basketball team, he got a ribbing from his brother.

Noah Riley, a quality control coach and analyst for the NFL’s New York Giants, gave him a hard time: Our teams are way tougher.

Back then, Noah was likely referring to the two problems that have plagued Riley’s first two WSU teams: Turnovers and defense. The Cougars finished last season ranked No. 292 in turnover rate and No. 248 in effective field goal percentage defense, painting a picture of an undisciplined, mistake-prone club.

Ahead of Riley’s third season at WSU, which begins with a home matchup against Davidson at 6 p.m. Monday, can the Cougars reverse those trends?

“Well, I think it starts in practice,” said Riley, whose team plays just five home nonconference games this season. “With our teams in the past that have won championships and won a lot of games, there’s been chippy practices, and it’s uncomfortable. And you walk away from practice with just a little bit of uncomfortableness because someone had to lose. I think that’s something that we’ve taken away this year.”

In the first year of the rebuilt Pac-12, WSU will use a retooled roster with 14 newcomers to try and turn around the problems that afflicted the last two Cougar teams. As they head into Monday’s season opener, they’ll likely start the same group that fueled their team’s second and final exhibition game, a road win over rival Washington last week.

That will likely mean lots of touches for East Texas A&M transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, who tallied a team-best 23 points and 11 rebounds in that game, plus opportunities for Central Missouri transfer guard Lazerek Houston and Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips, each of whom scored in double figures. The rest of the Cougs’ starting lineup figures to include UNLV transfer big man Ladji Dembele and Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, whose size could make a difference for a WSU team that has struggled to rebound the past two seasons.

Against Davidson, which was picked to finish eighth of 14 teams in the Atlantic 10 preseason poll, WSU will likely need some more of that recipe. The Cougars played an ugly game to beat the Huskies . The game featured a combined 87 free throws, and neither team shot better than 40% from the field . But they did make nine 3-pointers. They got five combined from Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell and former Eastern Washington wing Casey Jones, who spent the last two years on a church mission.

From a 30,000-foot view, that’s the main contingent that the Cougars will use to replace several key offseason losses, including several to the transfer portal: Ace Glass (Vanderbilt), forward ND Okafor (Mississippi State) and wing Ri Vavers (Memphis), plus guards Jerone Morton (Kentucky) and Tomas Thrastarson (Seattle U), forward Eemeli Yalaho (NC State) and key reserve Parker Gerrits (Wyoming).

This WSU team features only two returners, forward Dominik Robinson and walk-on guard Dio Blakely, which means most of the minutes will belong to transfers. A few other names to watch include TCU transfer RJ Jones and French freshman forward Mohamed Sankhe.

Sankhe totaled five points and three rebounds in 15 minutes against UW.

Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins also figures to make a splash, but because an injury sidelined him for both exhibition games, it’s unclear when he’ll be able to get on the court.

“We’ve got a lot of new faces, and so it’s been a really busy preseason for us trying to get in some concepts,” Riley said. “I think we simplified a few things to make sure that we’re able to play together and play hard, and I think that’s something that just takes time. And I think we’re learning those lessons.”

How David Riley’s Washington State basketball team adjusted after another mass exodus last season
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – After David Riley wrapped up his second season at the helm of Washington State’s men’s basketball program in April, he may have felt like he was having deja vu.

For the second straight year, his entire starting five had departed. For the second straight year, he would have to rebuild an entire roster from scratch. He’d have to do it all via the transfer portal, which had claimed each of the top scorers from his first two WSU teams.

So headed into his third season, the Cougars’ basketball roster looks almost entirely brand new, as it has each of the two years that preceded it. Gone are Ace Glass and ND Okafor, two staples of last year’s WSU team, as are all but two players from that team.

Riley spent much of the spring and summer constructing the roster for this 2026-27 team, which kicks off its season Monday at home against Davidson, one of the rare nonconference games at Beasley Coliseum to open the season.

Before that happens, though, let’s revisit how Riley’s third WSU team came together, the players, the fits and how it all rounded into shape for the Cougars. The good news for Riley: In late March and early April, before the transfer portal officially opened, many of the WSU players who planned on leaving announced their plans to do so. The Cougars knew the players they would have to replace and had more time to scour the portal for new fill-ins.

That stands in stark contrast to last spring, when the players leaving WSU didn’t make that decision until after the portal opened, leaving coaches with less time to find their replacements.

WSU’s team includes 14 newcomers, including nine from the transfer portal: Texas A&M transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, Northwestern transfer forward Tyler Kropp, Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Central Missouri (D-II) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, TCU transfer guard RJ Jones, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins, Manhattan transfer forward Fraser Roxburgh, UNLV transfer forward Ladji Dembele and Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips.

Riley’s third roster also includes wing Casey Jones, who last played for Riley at Eastern Washington before taking the next two years off for a church mission, as well as Spanish guard Pedro Sancho Moraga, French forward Mohamed Sankhe Golden State Prep product Roman Stathis, freshman Brayden Kyman and returners Dominik Robinson and Dio Blakely.

“We’ve got a lot of new faces, and so it’s been a really busy preseason for us, trying to get in some concepts,” Riley said in late October. “I think we simplified a few things to make sure that we’re able to play together and play hard, and I think that’s something that just takes time. And I think we’re learning those lessons. I think we have more aggression, a little more confidence than last year.”

The Cougars’ first commitment of the offseason came courtesy of Roxburgh, who came over from Manhattan College in New York City, where he started in 31 of 32 games, averaging 11 points and 5.8 rebounds per game. Roxburgh also shot 44% from the field, including 32% from beyond the arc on four attempts per game.

He figures to play a stretch four role, not unlike that of former forward Simon Hildebrandt, who played for last year’s WSU team. In Roxburgh’s commitment, it became clear that Riley and coaches value some versatility at their small forward or power forward spots.

“I think when I was still at Eastern, we were looking at him more as a three-four,” Riley said in the spring. “He’s another guy who just brings a ton of versatility to the game. Can pass, can think the game.”

WSU coaches’ second addition of the offseason came from Houston, who lit up the Division II ranks last season, averaging 20.8 points, four rebounds and five assists on 46.2% shooting, including 37% from 3-point territory. A quick ball-handler and crafty finisher, Houston’s finalists included one of WSU’s future Pac-12 opponents, Boise State.

“On my visit, it kinda felt like a family,” Houston said. “Just talking to the coaches, it wasn’t awkward. I didn’t feel like I gotta portray myself as somebody else. I felt like I could be myself, talk to them, and I just felt like it was like a good community. And I wanted to be a part of that.”

Around the same time, Riley picked up commitments from two other players who figure to play cornerstone roles on this team, Akins and Harrison. Akins started his career at Denver before playing last season at Wake Forest, where he averaged 5.3 points in 15.2 minutes per game, starting in eight games.

Harrison started his career at Tarleton State before spending last season at East Texas A&M, where he averaged 14.7 points and 6.1 rebounds in 30 minutes per game, starting 28 of 30 games. He also shot an efficient 53% inside the arc.

“Ronnie is a guy that’s super talented,” Riley said. “Bigger than he looks on film. He came up on his visit, and just a big body, strong, really just a confident player that can do a little bit of everything.”

That’s also around the same time when Riley secured a commitment from Kropp, a transfer from Northwestern, where fans seemed disappointed to lose him. Starting 10 games that season, he averaged 3.1 points and 2.1 rebounds per game.

Other staples on this WSU team figure to include Phillips and Dembele, who joined Kropp, Houston and Harrison in the Cougars’ starting lineup for their exhibition opener, a 92-64 loss to New Mexico in October. Phillips profiles as a scoring guard, while Dembele provides some physicality underneath and some upside around the arc, where he can shoot it from 3.

Can that group help Riley put a forgettable season in the rearview mirror? It might help that over the offseason, his brother, Noah, gave David a hard time. “Our teams are way tougher,” Noah would say, referring to his New York Giants, where he works as a quality control coach.

Whether or not that’s true, what can David do to turn around that perception this season?

“I think it starts in practice,” Riley said. “With our teams in the past that have won championships and won a lot of games, there’s been chippy practices, and it’s uncomfortable. And you walk away from practice with just a little bit of uncomfortableness because someone had to lose. I think that’s something that we’ve taken away this year.”

Washington State.title: David Riley, Washington State enter rebuilt Pac-12 with immense roster turnover
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – When he looks back, David Riley realizes that in his first pair of years as Washington State’s head coach, he hasn’t let his players scrimmage each other in practice as much as he should have.

In those days, he ran his guys through all kinds of drills, all manner of concepts. That approach may have helped in its own right, but as Riley prepares for his third season with the Cougars, he wants to put players in more live situations. He wants to learn what makes each one tick, create more pressure situations.

After all, Riley figures, what happens if the first adversity WSU faces comes in its Nov. 2 season opener against Davidson?

“That’s a problem,” Riley said.

In their first season of the rebuilt Pac-12, the Cougars will try to avoid the ones that plagued them in their previous two years under Riley, whose teams couldn’t avoid turnovers or guard well enough. This year, with 14 newcomers and nine from the transfer portal, WSU has a chance to turn those around in a convincing way.

The Cougars opened the season with two exhibition matchups, a road loss to New Mexico and a road win over rival Washington, the latter of which can provide a window into how this team might operate. The key cogs in this group will involve East Texas A&M transfer wing Ronnie Harrison, whose two-way acumen figures to make him a weapon on both ends of the court, as well as Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips and Central Missouri (D-II) transfer guard Lazerek Houston, all of whom scored in double figures in their team’s win over UW.

This WSU team features only two returners, forward Dominik Robinson and walk-on guard Dio Blakely, which means most of the minutes will belong to transfers. Coaches had to hit the transfer portal to replace key players from last year’s team, including guard Ace Glass (Vanderbilt), forward ND Okafor (Mississippi State) and wing Ri Vavers (Memphis), plus guards Jerone Morton (Kentucky) and Tomas Thrastarson (Seattle U), forward Eemeli Yalaho (NC State) and key reserve Parker Gerrits (Wyoming).

So how will the Cougars’ new group mesh? That much will depend on Harrison, Phillips and Houston, as well as Providence transfer wing Jaylen Harrell, Northwestern transfer big man Tyler Kropp, Wake Forest transfer guard Sebastian Akins and UNLV transfer forward Ladji Dembele. Former Eastern Washington wing Casey Jones, who spent the last two years on a church mission, is also back playing for Riley.

“There definitely is some differences when you have guys that have played in your system before and you know what’s returning, how to build around that,” Riley said. “For us, I think that’s the beauty of how we play. We’re pretty versatile. We’ve had teams that have been really good with guards, with bigs, with wings. I think being multidimensional is really important for us, and getting that physicality was something that we really wanted to embrace. I think we did that. Now it’s time to figure out how it all gels.”

The Cougars won’t get much of an easy on-ramp into the season. Including its season opener, a Nov. 2 home matchup with Davidson, WSU plays only four Division-I nonconference home games, the program’s fewest since the 1973-74 seasons. It highlights the way coaches like Riley have to keep the team budget in mind when building schedules, trying to generate revenue via buy games that can be used in a multitude of ways.

Here’s a sample of WSU’s nonconference schedule: at High Point on Nov. 7, at Duquesne on Nov. 10, against Duke in California on Nov. 21, at Murray State on Nov. 30, at Weber State on Dec. 9 and at LSU on Dec. 28. The Cougs will be away from Pullman more than this program ever has been since the ’70s. Couple that with the team’s new-look roster and you understand the challenges facing the Cougars.

And that’s to make no mention of the reimagined Pac-12, whose best sport might be men’s hoops. The Cougs will host No. 15 Gonzaga in early January, during their university’s winter break, and a February road stretch against Gonzaga and San Diego State will prove tough. WSU also has a road date with Utah State set up for late January. If it’s not a gauntlet, it’s something close.

It’s not easy for any team, let alone one like WSU, which has turned over its entire starting five each of the last two seasons.

“I’d say that was probably the biggest thing for us in the off-season – we had so many new guys,” Kropp said. “We just saw what a team like New Mexico with so many returners, how valuable it is and how valuable that chemistry is. That was just a big focus for us in the off-season. As soon as we got on campus, we made sure, as often as we could, whenever we had an off-day, we were together.”

To turn things around from last season, when the Cougars went 12-20 overall and 7-11 in their second and final season as West Coast Conference affiliate members, they will have to shore up two things most of all: Defense and turnovers. A year ago, WSU turned it over on about 18% of its possessions, which ranked No. 292 nationally. That group also allowed opponents to register an effective field goal percentage of 53%, which was No. 248 in the country.

So what’s the key to reversing those fortunes? Riley likes to say it involves identifying selfless players.

“I think that starts in the recruiting process, is getting guys who want to play this kind of basketball, who want to play a team style offensively and defensively, want to be physical and disruptive, and I think we did a good job of that,” Riley said. “We’re getting guys that understand the importance of that, and like I said earlier, I think once you really understand how we play, it’s impossible to do it alone.”

Washington State.title: Pac-12 preview: New-look conference should provide stiff challenges, hostile road arenas
Washington State.summary:
On Sept. 16, Utah State announced the school had sold out tickets for Gonzaga’s inaugural trip to Dee Glen Smith Spectrum. That wouldn’t necessarily be news – certainly not Gonzaga’s first time drawing a standing room-only crowd on the road – but the announcement arrived two full weeks before the Pac-12 Conference released its schedule, meaning more than 10,000 fans purchased tickets without knowing a concrete date for the Jan. 21 matchup.

Gonzaga can expect bigger crowds and more robust challenges in the new conference, which should test the Bulldogs top-to-bottom in a way the West Coast Conference didn’t and help Mark Few’s avoid the resume dings that were often inevitable in January and February.

The reimagined Pac-12 may not be ready to compete with the SEC, Big Ten, Big 12, ACC and Big East on Selection Sunday, but this new group of nine isn’t lacking credentials.

Gonzaga and San Diego State bring three combined national championship appearances over the last nine years with 31 combined NCAA Tournament victories sprinkled in during that span. Utah State is in the middle of the school’s best run, punching six NCAA tickets over the last eight seasons, including each of the last four. Boise State made three straight March Madness trips before recent misses and Colorado State has been exceptional in its own right, qualifying in 2022, 2024 and 2025. Oregon State and Washington State both made semirecent NCAA appearances under the Pac-12’s old flag.

This new-look Pac-12 might have been a candidate to get three teams into the previous NCAA Tournament, but the expanded 76-team bracket provides a pathway to one or two additional bids.

Regardless, college hoops fans out West should have plenty of dates to circle on the new Pac-12 calendar – not just the one taking place Jan. 21 in Logan, Utah.

1. Gonzaga

Coach: Mark Few (772-156), 28th year at Gonzaga

2025-26 record: 31-4. WCC: 16-2, tied-first

Key newcomers: C Massamba Diop (7-1, 230), G Isiah Harwell (6-6, 220), G Nathan De Sousa (6-2, 192), F Izan Almansa (6-10, 200/eligibility pending), G Xaivian Lee (6-4, 185), F Chauncey Wiggins (6-11, 225/eligibility pending), G Javon Bennett (5-10, 165/eligibility pending)

Key losses: F Graham Ike, G Tyon Grant-Foster, G Jalen Warley, F Emmanuel Innocenti, G Mario Saint-Supery, G Adam Miller, G Braeden Smith, C Ismaila Diagne

Outlook: Despite the various curveballs this offseason has tossed their way, the Zags are still the favorites – considerable favorites, maybe – to capture a Pac-12 crown next spring. They’ve assembled one of the country’s top frontcourts, blending Braden Huff’s offensive touch with Massamba Diop’s rim protection. This should be a second-weekend team with a Final Four ceiling if Xaivian Lee, Javon Bennett and Chauncey Wiggins stay/become eligible.

2. Utah State

Coach: Ben Jacobson (397-259), 1st year at Utah State

2025-26 record: 29-7. Mountain West: 15-5, first

Key newcomers: Dallin Hall (6-4, 200/eligibility pending), Connor Turnbull (6-11, 225), AJ Bates (6-4, 200), Solomon Callaghan (6-2, 195), Will Hornseth (6-9, 235), Collin Mulholland (6-11, 240)

Key losses: G MJ Collins Jr., G Drake Allen, G Kolby King, F Garry Clark, F Adlan Elamin, G Elijah Perryman

Outlook: Constant coaching turnover hasn’t impacted the Aggies, who’ve been to four consecutive NCAA Tournaments under three different coaches. Utah State has a solid chance to get there again under Ben Jacobson, who made five NCAA appearances over 20 seasons at Northern Iowa. The Aggies will lean heavily on veteran forward Mason Falslev, the favorite to earn Pac-12 MVP honors if the award doesn’t go to a Gonzaga player. Frontcourt mate and reigning Mountain West Sixth Man of the Year Karson Templin is another solid all-conference candidate.

3. San Diego State

Coach: Brian Dutcher (220-79), 10th year at San Diego State

2025-26 record: 22-11. Mountain West: 13-6, second

Key newcomers: G Chance Gladden (6-4, 192), G Isaiah Sy (6-6, 200), F Bear Cherry (6-10, 270), G David Torresani (6-2, 168), G Zach White (6-5, 208), F Luca Vincini (6-10, 242)

Key losses: F Magoon Gwath, F Pharaoh Compton, G Miles Byrd, G BJ Davis, G Taj DeGourville, G Reese Dixon-Waters, F Miles Heide

Outlook: This won’t be Brian Dutcher’s strongest roster on paper, but we’ll give the benefit of the doubt to a coach who’s been part of four Mountain West regular-season or tournament championships and six NCAA Tournament appearances since taking over for Steve Fisher. Elzie Harrington, the team’s only returning starter, is a proficient 3-point shooter, but the Aztecs may also require a lot from transfers Chance Gladden (Boston U), Bear Cherry (Sacramento State) and Isaiah Sy (Oregon State), especially in the wake of Nick Anderson’s offseason knee injury.

4. Oregon State

Coach: Justin Joyner (0-0), 1st season at Oregon State

2025-26 record: 17-16. WCC: 9-9, tie-fourth

Key newcomers: F Jackson Rasmussen (6-9, 211), G Legend Smiley (6-5, 188), G Daniel Freitag (6-2, 192), F DeShawn Gory (6-6, 169), C Xavion Staton (7-1, 224), G Chris Johnson (6-5, 189), C Dennis Evans (7-2, 231)

Key losses: F Isaiah Sy, G Dez White, F Johan Munch, C Yaak Yaak, F Jorge Diaz Graham, F Olavi Suutela

Outlook: Justin Joyner, a national title-winning assistant with years of experience building scouting reports for Gonzaga, takes over Oregon State’s program after Wayne Tinkle’s tenure ended. Joyner lacks head-coaching experience, but he’s assembled a roster that looks talented enough on paper to compete with the top half of the Pac-12. Program veteran Josiah Lake II brings leadership and ball-handling, while transfers DeShawn Gory (Fresno State) and Daniel Freitag (Buffalo) have a chance to lead the Beavers in scoring. Similar to the Michigan team Joyner worked for last season, OSU should be massive up front with three 7-footers on this roster.

5. Colorado State

Coach: Ali Farokhmanesh (21-13), second season at Colorado State

2025-26 record: 21-13. Mountain West: 11-9, seventh

Key newcomers: G Justin Menard (6-3, 185), F Jaden Ghoreishi (6-9, 215), Amondo Miller Jr. (6-7, 195)

Key losses: F Brandon Rechsteiner, G Jevin Muniz, F Augustinas Kiudulas

Outlook: The Rams lose their top scorer from a year ago, but return players who ranked second, third, fourth, sixth and seventh in points per game. It’s a level of retention that’s hard to come by in the current college basketball climate and one of the primary reasons Ali Farokhmanesh’s group might be a step ahead of others in the Pac-12 when the regular season begins. Marist transfer Justin Menard slides into the starting lineup next to a quartet of returners that includes three double-digit scorers in Kyle Jorgensen (11.5 ppg), Carey Booth (10.7 ppg) and Josh Pascarelli (10.2 ppg). Spokane’s Jaden Ghoreishi could see minutes off the bench as a freshman.

6. Boise State

Coach: Leon Rice (336-189), 17th season at Boise State

2025-26 record: 20-12. Mountain West: 12-8, tie-fifth

Key newcomers: F Dovydas Butka (6-9, 225), G Ty Rodgers (6-6, 205), G Lamar Washington (6-4, 210/eligibility pending), G Damari Wheeler-Thomas (6-0, 190).

Key losses: F Javan Buchanan, F Drew Fielder, G Dylan Andrews, F Andrew Meadow, F Dominic Parolin

Outlook: Former Gonzaga assistant Leon Rice faces a tall task replacing Boise State’s four double-digit scorers from a year ago, especially after an offseason injury to Ty Rodgers sidelined the Illinois transfer indefinitely. Campbell’s Dovydas Butka is a nightly double-double threat while North Dakota State transfer Damari Wheeler-Thomas is expected to take on primary ball-handling duties. Returning reserves Julian Bowie and Aginaldo Neto both had 20-plus point performances in recent exhibitions against Idaho and Washington. If eligible, 5-in-5 Georgia Tech transfer Lamar Washington has a chance to be one of Boise State’s top scorers, rebounders and facilitators.

7. Texas State

Coach: Terrence Johnson (107-81), seventh season at Texas State

2025-26 record: 19-13. Sun Belt: 11-7, tie-second

Key newcomers: G Quel’Ron House (6-0, 180), G KJ Younger (6-4, 218), F Ronald Jessamy (6-8, 220), G Caleb Steger (6-5, 180)

Key losses: G Franck Emmou, G Jaelyn Lee, C Tay Knox, G Deke Thompson, F Isaiah Barganier, G Cameron Simpson

Outlook: DJ Hall is one of the best-kept secrets in midmajor basketball and should be at the top of every Texas State scouting report this season after averaging 15.6 points, 7.7 rebounds and 1.4 steals as a freshman. The Bobcats have continuity beyond Hall, though, and managed to bring back second-leading scorer Mark Drone (14.2 ppg), assists/steals leader Kaden Gumbs (3.0 apg, 1.9 spg) and guard Dimp Pernell, who made 40.6% of his 3-pointers before a season-ending injury. Southern Illinois transfer Quel’Ron House will have a chance to be one of Texas State’s top two-way players.

8. Washington State

Coach: David Riley (93-73), third season at Washington State

2025-26 record: 12-20. WCC: 7-11, eighth

Key newcomers: G Lazerek Houston (6-0, 155), F Ronnie Harrison (6-8, 210), F Fraser Roxburgh (6-7, 215), G Sebastian Akins (6-2, 175), F Ladji Dembele (6-8, 255), G Jaylen Harrell (6-5, 210), F Tyler Kropp (6-9, 230), G Jamari Phillips (6-4, 190), G R.J. Jones, 6-2, 189 (2.6 ppg, 0.4 rpg).

Key losses: G Ace Glass, G Rihards Vavers, F ND Okafor, F Eeemeli Yalaho, G Tomas Thrastarson, G Jerone Morton, F Emmanuel Ugbo, G Kase Wynott, G Adria Rodriguez, G Parker Gerrits.

Outlook: The Cougars lost 98.9% of their scoring from 2025-26 – only Dio Blakely’s 0.8 points per game return – and are easily the most challenging team to handicap a year later. With an all-new starting lineup and rotation, it’s wise not to read too deeply into WSU’s 92-64 exhibition loss at New Mexico, but also means David Riley’s squad could face growing pains through a challenging nonconference schedule that sends the Cougs outside of Pullman 11 times in November and December. Division II standout Lazerek Houston and East Texas A&M Ronnie Harrison both hit double digits on efficient shooting in the exhibition loss, with Harrison scoring 23 in Sunday’s 84-80 exhibition win at Washington.

9. Fresno State

Coach: Vance Walberg (33-80), third season at Fresno State

2025-26 record: 13-19. Mountain West: 7-13, 10th

Key newcomers: G Dragos Lungu (6-6, 180), G Ross Candelino (6-5, 198), F Bradey Henige (7-0, 240), G Brian Amuneke (6-5, 184), C Baye Fall (6-11, 205), G Quentin Rhymes (6-6, 195), G KJ Perry (6-3, 180)

Key losses: G Jake Heidbreder, F Deshawn Gory, F Jac Mani, G David Douglas Jr., C Wilson Jacques, G Zaon Collins, G Cameron Faas, C Gasper Kocevar, G Bastien Rieber

Outlook: Washington State and Fresno State face the biggest rebuilds and not surprisingly are the teams occupying the final two spots in our predictions. But there could be a sizable gap between the Cougars and Bulldogs, who are separated by 60 spots in Ken Pomeroy’s preseason ratings. Fresno State lost every contributor from last year and could rely heavily on guards Dragos Lungu, a 13.8 ppg scorer at UT Martin, and Ross Candelino, who averaged 11.2 ppg at Libscomb to lead them in the scoring column. The Bulldogs will have to turn things around after settling for a 19-45 record over Vance Walberg’s first two seasons.

Washington State.title: How a quiet spring allowed the Washington State women to focus on continuity
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – For Washington State women’s basketball coach Kamie Ethridge, the word continuity has a significant meaning this fall.

Two years removed from losing six players to the transfer portal and having to do a roster makeover, the Cougars welcome back all their starters and even a sixth who started 20 games.

The Cougars may not have the seasoning that Gonzaga’s returning five starters possess, but they believe there will be significant improvement in 2026-27.

Washington State showed it was heading in the right direction at the end of last season, winning four of its final five to finish 9-25 – the worst season under the ninth-year coach.

Ethridge and the Cougars are focused on wiping the sour taste of last year out of their mouths.

“I really feel good about this team,” Ethridge said. “The leadership of our older players has been unbelievably good.”

Ethridge spent less time in the transfer portal last spring, bringing in one player – 6-foot-2 sophomore forward Elizaveta (Lizzie) Filchagina, who spent a year at SMU.

The quiet spring was a respite considering the chaos that was created with six departures the year before.

“Now it’s so much about, can you get buy-in from your team and can you get players who are willing to just really live in the process,” Ethridge said.

Ethridge said it will be interesting to see how the new 5-in-5 eligibility format plays out. In the past, coaches used redshirt seasons to allow new, raw players time to adjust and develop. Now the eligibility clock is running as soon as freshmen arrive on campus.

Players on rosters before the eligibility change get an extra year if they haven’t used a redshirt season previously.

“The process may mean you don’t get to play much your freshman year,” Ethridge said. “The fear is still out there that they’re not gonna wait and they’re gonna be impatient and they’re gonna leave after one year when they don’t get exactly what they want. So it’s still so much about, can we prove ourselves as coaches and as a program and that we really show we can develop players and that they’re getting better year after year.”

Ethridge has a different recruiting strategy, panning for players internationally. Nine of 12 players on WSU’s roster are internationals. It has become a more attractive avenue to find players because of the name, image and likeness element.

She has no problem paying players within reason after they have proven their value. And if WSU can’t match what players may acquire elsewhere then the door is open for them to do so.

Ethridge wants players who buy into her culture.

“We have to make sure our culture is growing in a real positive way to make sure people want to be in this program,” Ethridge said.

Player retention in the offseason tells Ethridge her program is headed in the right direction after the hiccup two years ago.

Two of WSU’s three seniors arrived as freshmen – guard Eleonora Villa from Lissone, Italy, and post Alex Covill from Missoula. The third senior, guard Mackenzie Chatfield, transferred from Western Kentucky last year. Her eligibility is over after this season because she used a redshirt after enrolling at WKU from Auckland, New Zealand.

WSU brought in three freshmen, one from Belgium and one from Argentina, and one from Oregon. A redshirt freshman hails from France.

Sophomores Malia Ruud, from Pasco, and Tanja Valancic, from Slovenia, arrived last year and earned starting time. Sophomore Malvina Haziri (Kosovo) saw limited minutes last year.

The lone junior, Charlotte Abraham (France), started last year.

The Cougars have commitments from two more internationals in the class of 2027. Ethridge continues to tap into that pipeline, something she hopes will serve WSU well in the rebuilt Pac-12.

Washington State.title: Washington State women ready for bounce-back season in new Pac-12
Washington State.summary:
PULLMAN – Kamie Ethridge expects her Washington State University women’s basketball team to be much improved in 2026-27.

Whether that’s enough to put a 9-25 record last year in the rearview mirror remains to be seen.

Count senior point guard Mackenzie Chatfield as one thoroughly motivated by what transpired a year ago.

When asked what drove her during the offseason, Chatfield cracked, “Losing 30 games. That probably hit me really hard.”

A slight exaggeration but point well made.

“Last year was last year,” Chatfield said. “I have to be better for this group, be better for my teammates. We were here all summer and we grinded it out together. Knowing that this is my last year and I only have one more shot at it, I’m gonna give it my all no matter what.”

Chatfield said being with this team makes it easy to want to change things.

“You want to go to war with these girls, and they’re so capable of great things,” Chatfield said.

Including Chatfield, who transferred from Western Kentucky last year. But a strange thing happened to her near the end of her time there. She lost all confidence in her 3-point shooting – not because of a fundamental flaw in her shooting touch but because of a shoe that caused nerve damage to a foot, Ethridge said.

Chatfield made 28 of 80 shots behind the 3-point line (35%), but she only attempted one last season for the Cougars.

She spent the offseason retraining herself.

“It’s something that I have worked really hard on,” Chatfield said. “It’s all mental. Like when you’re able to do something in your sleep and you can’t do that again and then you have to try to relearn something. I don’t know how many hours me and Laurie (Koehn, assistant coach) have spent together. So just trusting the process and trusting the work. I don’t want that to be solely what I’m capable of. I want to still be able to play in multiple ways.”

She averaged 4.6 points, 3.5 rebounds and 3.3 assists per game. Those are numbers that should increase measurably this season.

Chatfield will have lots of help. The Cougars return all five starters and a sixth when counting Malia Ruud, who had 20 starts as a true freshman last year.

Senior guard Eleonora Villa, an All-West Coast Conference second-team pick, led WSU with 16.5 points. Senior Alex Covill, who missed 14 games dealing with a foot injury, averaged 10.8 points and 4.5 rebounds.

At 6-foot-6, Covill will be expected to have more of a scoring presence inside and on the boards.

The other returning starters are junior guard Charlotte Abraham (10.3 ppg, 6.2 rpg) and sophomore forward Tanja Valancic (3.3 ppg, 3.2 rebounds), who started 25 games.

Ethridge is thankful for the experience.

“It’s amazing what a year forward means,” Ethridge said. “There’s a lot of comfort in the older players. All the older players got better and I feel very secure about them.”

The biggest question marks are among the six new names to the roster. Most of the new blood comes in the form of three freshmen – four when including a redshirt freshman.

The four freshmen and two sophomores, including 6-2 SMU transfer forward Elizaveta (Lizzie) Filchagina , will battle for minutes off the bench.

Ethridge has noticed three specific things in preseason practices that are encouraging.

“We are a little more balanced,” she said. “We are a little more physical than we’ve been in years past. We communicate better than we have in the past.”

Still, Ethridge knows consistent offense will cure a lot of ills.

“It’s still a shot-making game and a decision-making game,” Ethridge said. “We are really good some days and maybe not as good other days.”

Villa and Covill will command much attention from opponents. Villa scored a career-high 560 points last season, reaching double figures in 30 of 34 games.

Covill, who has struggled with injuries throughout her career, says she’s healthy and ready to go.

“We have learned a lot of lessons from the years before, especially last year, and the returners have come into this year wanting to change some things and create a new dynamic,” Covill said. “And we’re thankful we have newbies coming in as well. They’re following along and want to work hard and get better every day.”

Said Ethridge: “It’s (early). With the pieces that we have, we have a chance to be pretty good in January, February. But we’ve got to grow them fast and need everybody bought in and believing in what we’re doing here.”

Washington State.title: Gonzaga, even in new league, remain title favorites | Pac-12 women
Washington State.summary:
Pac-12 women’s basketball most likely will be divided into three tiers in the reconditioned conference.

Gonzaga and San Diego State should occupy the top two spots by season’s end.

Third through sixth – featuring Washington State, Colorado State, Oregon State and Boise State – will be highly competitive but could finish in any order.

And the three lowest places should be decided between Utah State, Fresno State and Texas State.

If Gonzaga plays as advertised, though, the Zags could make it a solo run to a conference championship, creating a fourth tier.

The Zags are expected to carry over their West Coast Conference dominance into the Pac-12.

Gonzaga is ranked No. 49 in the Bart Torvik preseason analytical data – the highest ranking for a non-Power Four conference school. Oregon State is 69th, Colorado State 80th and San Diego State 97th.

Here’s a look at the predicted order of finish:

1. Gonzaga. Easy, easy choice here.

None of the nine conference teams bring back a roster as deep as the Zags. Junior forward Lauren Whittaker, who dominated in the WCC and was named the Player of the Year and Freshman of the Year last season, is expected to pick up where she left off. She’s the runaway pick as the Pac-12’s Player of the Year. Whittaker has plenty of support down low. Couple that with a perimeter that features the top 3-point shooting team in the nation a year ago and opponents will have to pick their poison in what they try to defend.

2. San Diego State. The Aztecs cruised to the Mountain West regular-season championship last year, stumbling once in 20 games. They were upset in the conference tournament, but extended their season in the WBIT where they were eliminated in the quarterfinals. SDSU has four of five starters back and add four transfers and three freshmen. The Aztecs finished 27-6 overall, tying the record for most wins in a season.

3. Oregon State. The Beavers can match up with any guards in the conference, but they sorely lack an experienced inside presence. OSU returns WCC All-Conference First Team picks Jenna Villa and Kennedie Shuler, both senior guards. Shuler was named the WCC Defensive Player of the Year and is arguably the best point guard in the conference. Villa, a transfer a year ago from Washington State, averaged 14.9 points in a breakout season.

4. Colorado State. The Rams won the MW Tournament last year, advancing to the NCAA Tournament where they showed well in a 65-62 loss to Michigan State and finished 27-8. CSU returns just one starter and bring in eight players including five transfers. The Rams have thrived in recent seasons on transfers.

5. Washington State. The Cougars have much to prove, but have a strong foundation. They return five starters – six if you count Malia Rudd, who started 20 games as a freshman. Leading the way is senior 5-8 guard Eleonora Villa, a second team All-WCC selection. The Italy native averaged a career-high 16.5 points and 3.6 assists while playing 34.8 minutes a game.

6. Boise State. The Broncos were highly competitive in the MW a year ago, finishing 25-9 overall and 14-6 in league. They must replace four starters. Coach Gordy Presnell begins his 39th season as a head coach, 21st at BSU. He’s six wins shy of 800 (794-392). The retooling will include three transfers and four freshmen.

7. Fresno State. The Bulldogs have much work ahead. They bring back one starter from a team that finished 15-18. The Bulldogs have brought in eight transfers and three freshmen. They get the nod here over Texas State based on playing in a tougher conference previously.

8. Texas State. The Bobcats have the lone new head coach in Chris Kielsmeier. He was previously a head coach at Cleveland State, Wayne State College and Howard Payne. Texas State brings back two starters. Kielsmeier signed eight transfers.

9. Utah State. The Aggies might as well be starting from rock bottom. They lost 18 straight to end last year after a 6-6 start. They return two starters, but wholesale changes are expected with six transfers.

Washington State.title: An uncertain future for an Apple Cup hoops rivalry that only one side wants to preserve
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – The hoops version of the Apple Cup is unrecognizable these days.

Washington and Washington State have been playing against each other since 1910 and have matched up in 301 games, which is one of the oldest and most played series in men’s college basketball.

In front of 7,011 fans at Alaska Airlines Arena, the two teams met once again Sunday afternoon, and the Huskies lost 84-80 in an exhibition in a rivalry that used to mean something.

“Rivalries in college basketball, it’s tough,” said former UW star Isaiah Thomas who watched from stands below his No. 2 jersey, which hangs in the rafters. “It’s a different time, day and age.”

The 37-year-old Thomas talked to the Huskies before the game and tried to explain the importance of the UW-WSU rivalry to a team comprised of 12 newcomers born outside of the state, including five international players.

“It’s just human nature if you’re not from here to be a little clueless about the Apple Cup and what that really means,” Thomas said. “All these games probably feel the same, but just reminding them that it’s not about you the individual. It’s about the program, the city and the state rivalry.

“You just understand it more and more the longer you’re here. My job is to show them that it does mean something no matter if it’s a game that counts or not.”

Did they receive the message?

“If we win, they did,” Thomas said smiling at halftime. “If we lose, they didn’t.”

None of the current Cougars played in last year’s 81-69 loss while Wesley Yates III, Lathan Sommerville and Jasir Rencher suited up for the Huskies.

“I’ve coached two of their guys more than either of us have coached an entire team,” WSU coach David Riley said referring to UW’s Steele Venters and LeJuan Watts. “It’s a weird deal.”

Riley coached Venters at Eastern Washington and led Watts at EWU and at WSU.

“This is always a fun game, but I’ve never won so maybe it’s me,” Watts said smiling, referring to his 0-2 Apple Cup record, including an 89-73 WSU loss on Dec. 18, 2024, when he tallied 15 point, eight rebounds and three assists. “There’s no little brother thing (at Washington). That’s kind of what it was on the other side, just being the underdog.

“It’s a lot more drive and motivation if you’re Wazzu. I mean, you don’t have anything to lose.”

Despite a game-high 28 points on 7-for-12 shooting from the field from Watts, Lathan Sommerville scoring 19 points and Nikola Dzepina adding 16 points and 12 rebounds, Washington lost control midway in the second half.

The Huskies led 50-43 when the Cougars took control for good with a 13-2 run to go up 56-52 following an alley-oop dunk from Ronnie Harrison, who finished with a team-high 23 points.

Washington State went up 79-71 with 46 seconds left when Washington made one last push and cut its deficit to 81-78 following Venters’ 3-pointer with 15 seconds left.

After WSU guard Casey Jones missed a couple of free throws, the Huskies had a chance to tie but Watts’ 3-point attempt was deflected and fell short.

When it was over, Riley admitted he’s not sure if the series will continue.

“I hope we can get them on the schedule for a real game next year,” he said. “We’re taking this thing day by day. There’s a lot going on. There’s a lot of changes in college basketball, so hopefully we can make it happen next year.”

The Cougars have ceded the fate of the Apple Cup to the Huskies because they’re struggling to remain financially viable even in the Pac-12.

Among its 16 nonconference matchups on the 2026-27 schedule, Washington State plays just five in Pullman and nine on the road against High Point, Duquesne, Hawaii, Duke, Murray State, Southern Illinois, Weber State, UNLV, Seattle U, Eastern Washington and LSU.

“Home games against lesser teams usually cost a lot of money, and we’re in a spot now where it’s like we’d rather spend some of that on our roster,” Riley said. “We’re in a tough spot. It’s hard to find home-and-home (deals), especially in Pullman. So, we’re going on the road a lot and that’s part of the deal where we’re just, we’re going to play anyone anywhere at any time. We have a hard schedule, and we’ll be hardened by the time conference play hits.”

UW coach Danny Sprinkle, who begins his third season with the Huskies, knows canceling series with traditional rivals Gonzaga, Seattle U and potentially Washington State, is unpopular with UW fans.

However, he has his reasons.

“I know I’ll get killed for not playing (the Cougars) this year, but with our schedule, I have to do what’s best for Washington basketball,” Sprinkle said. “Fitting them in at a certain time, it was hard with us going to the Maui and playing BYU and two other terrific teams. Already having Baylor coming here, going to Utah, and then a lot of people around here forget you’re playing 20 Big Ten games … and probably 18 of them are Quad 1 games against the hardest teams in the country. So, that takes a toll on you.”

Riley, who is close friends with Sprinkle, understands.

“I’ve known Danny a long time,” he said. “There’s only a couple friends I’ve got in this business and he’s one of them. … He’s a good coach, great guy and he has to do what’s best for his team.”

Still, he wants the Apple Cup to continue.

“Whatever they tell us, we’ll go play the game,” Riley said. “We’ll find a way to make it work because it’s important to me. It’s important to our fans. It’s a great game, and it’s worth preserving.”

Washington State.title: Washington State beats rival Washington in men's basketball exhibition
Washington State.summary:
SEATTLE – For the first time since 1917, the men’s basketball teams from Washington State and Washington won’t meet in the regular season. But the Cougars still got a shot at their bitter rivals in a preseason matchup, and made the most of it.

WSU topped UW 84-80 in an exhibition on Sunday at Alaska Airlines Arena – a preseason boost for a Cougars team that was coming off a 28-point exhibition loss at New Mexico on Oct. 18.

The 7,011 in attendance were treated to a free-throw shootout. The teams combined for 87 foul shots. WSU went 31 of 46 from the line and the Huskies shot 30 of 41 from the stripe. The teams both shot 22 of 56 from the field. WSU’s 9-for-26 mark from 3-point range – compared to UW’s 6-for-23 – gave the visitors the edge.

The Cougars trailed by 10 points midway through the first half, but used an 8-2 run to get back in it and took a 38-37 lead into halftime. The Huskies opened a seven-point lead about seven minutes into the second period before a Casey Jones 3 keyed a 13-2 WSU run that put the Cougars up by four.

WSU’s Ronnie Harrison scored back-to-back buckets on a tip-in and a dunk with just over five minutes left to break a tie. The Cougars led by as many as eight points with under a minute left before a UW rally, but WSU got a game-winning block from Harrison on LeJuan Watts’ game-tying 3-point attempt with six seconds left.

Harrison, a senior transfer forward from East Texas A&M, led the Cougs with 23 points and 11 rebounds, shooting 8 of 9 from the floor. Guard Lazerek Houston, a Central Missouri transfer, added 15 points. Oregon transfer guard Jamari Phillips chipped in 12 points. Providence transfer guard Jaylen Harrell scored 11 points and Jones, a former Eastern Washington standout, had 10 for the new-look Cougars, who had to entirely rebuild their roster this offseason.

Watts, a former WSU and EWU star who spent last season at Texas Tech, led the Huskies with 28 points, shooting 7 of 12 from the field and 12 of 13 from the foul line. Gonzaga transfer Steele Venters had three points for UW.

The Cougs open their regular season Nov. 2 at home against Davidson.

Washington State.title: Washington State hoops rolled by New Mexico in exhibition; Andrew Cook shines in EWU's win over CSU Bakersfield
Washington State.summary:
Mountain West Freshman of the Year and sophomore guard Jake Hall scored 22 points on 8 of 10 shooting and the University of New Mexico Lobos Men’s basketball team beat the Washington State Cougars 92-64 in an exhibition game at The Pit in Albuquerque, New Mexico on Sunday. 

The Cougars never really stood a chance after the Lobos went on an 8-2 run to start the game, and pulled away with a 16-0 run with just under 14 minutes left in the first half.

Midway through the second half, the Cougs trailed by 42 points 80-38, their largest deficit of the game. 

Uriah Tennette hit a 3-pointer on the Lobos’ first possession but East Texas A&M senior transfer guard Ronnie Harrison replied with a layup to make it 3-2. 

But the Lobos separated themselves with a 16-point surge in a four-minute span in the first period started by redshirt freshman Imran Suljanovic’s 3-pointer at 13 minutes, 47 seconds. 

The Cougars stopped the bleeding when Dembele stole the ball from Hall, and connected with Houston on a fastbreak to make it 30-16. But WSU couldn’t recover and found themselves in a 25-point deficit entering halftime. 

Houston led WSU with 14 points and two assists, and Harrison added 12 points, four rebounds, and four assists for the Cougs. 

Andrew Cook leads Eagles to close win over CSU Bakersfield 

After missing all of last season with an ankle injury, and uncertainty surrounding his college eligibility this year, Andrew Cook shined in his 2026 season debut with the Eastern Washington Eagles, leading all players with 24 points in a 71-65 exhibition victory against CSU Bakersfield Roadrunners at Reese Court in Cheney on Sunday. 

Cook also added five rebounds to go with three assists. He was also a defensive force with a block early in the first half and two steals, including a critical one late in the second half that helped the Eagles retake the lead with just over three minutes remaining. 

Down 58-56 with 4 minutes, 7 seconds remaining, Cook stole the ball and was fouled by Tom Koppens on the fastbreak. Cook made his first free throw, but missed the second. But returning redshirt junior forward Emmett Marquardt got the offensive rebound, and Cook converted the layup to make it 59-58. EWU never trailed again. 

After a close first five minutes, the Eagles scored six straight thanks to a 3-pointer from Isak Homelius and found themselves up by eight 15-7 midway through the first half – their largest lead of the game. 

But the Roadrunners marched back, regaining the lead with 5 minutes, 25 seconds left in the first period after Malachi Richardson missed his 3-pointer, and Jaden Alexander converted his shot to make it 23-21. 

EWU and CSU Bakersfield exchanged leads, and the Eagles entered halftime down three.

Washington State.summary:

Well, WSU head coach Kirby Moore finally did the thing, benching his starting quarterback Caden Pinnick and replacing him with redshirt freshman Owen Eshelman. It's a move that definitely had to happen ... but will it work? Oregon State appears to be pretty dang good, and the Cougars are likely going to need to pile up some points to keep up with the suddenly explosive Beavers.

We also talked about men's basketball (the kenpom rankings were unveiled over the weekend), beer, cross country(!), soccer, and volleyball. Additionally, we revisited WSU athletics' new contract with an AI company as more information has come to light about how it's being used
